The movement itself insists that international shipping is not the target of its advance, while Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdulsalam has said that trade through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remains safe and uninterrupted, even as restrictions against Saudi-linked shipping remain in place.
However, it’s not just about whether the Houthis are physically capable of closing the strait. They are acquiring a tool with which they can raise or lower the risks to commercial shipping in accordance with the political and military situation. This is turning Bab el-Mandeb from one sector of Yemen’s protracted war into a second lever of pressure within the confrontation surrounding Iran.
Two straits, one system of pressure
The main reason the Houthi advance has become so sensitive for the United States and its allies lies in its timing, coming as it is amid a direct confrontation with Iran, which is already facing intense American pressure on its maritime communications and oil exports. While Iran’s room for maneuver in the Strait of Hormuz is constrained by the presence of American and allied forces, a second potentially unstable maritime corridor on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula forces Washington to reckon with an entirely different theater of escalation at the same time. A substantial share of Gulf oil exports passes through Hormuz, while Bab el-Mandeb links the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and onward to the Suez Canal. Simultaneous instability in both straits could disrupt not only regional energy flows but the wider system of trade connecting Asia and Europe.
The result is a kind of geographic trap, with Hormuz on the eastern side of the Arabian Peninsula, where Tehran can directly influence the level of risk surrounding maritime traffic, and Bab el-Mandeb on the western side, where a movement aligned with Iran possesses a similar capacity. It would nevertheless be inaccurate to claim that Tehran now controls both straits, because Ansar Allah is not an extension of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, has its own political agenda and makes its decisions primarily in response to developments inside Yemen. Yet this degree of Houthi autonomy makes the coalescing model of two-pronged pressure so useful to Iran. Tehran does not need to expand the conflict geographically with its own forces when an allied movement is already acting in ways that serve broadly compatible interests and impose additional costs on a common adversary.
Iran does not need to order the closure of Bab el-Mandeb, because the mere possibility of a renewed crisis in the Red Sea is enough to force the US to prepare for another escalation scenario. Washington must then redistribute military resources, reinforce maritime security and factor the consequences into its calculations about global energy markets. In other words, the effectiveness of the pressure does not depend on whether either strait is completely shut. It depends on whether both can be made sufficiently unstable to force the US and its allies to spend more resources protecting them.
The Houthis are bargaining for more than Iran
Reducing the current offensive to Tehran’s interests alone would also be misleading, because for the Houthis themselves the widening regional crisis offers a rare opportunity to reshape the terms of their long confrontation with Saudi Arabia. For several years, negotiations between Riyadh and Sanaa have revolved around highly specific issues, including the full operation of Houthi-controlled ports, expanded access through Sanaa airport, salary payments to public-sector employees, infrastructure reconstruction, foreign trade and the gradual easing of restrictions that Ansar Allah describes as a blockade. These demands lie at the heart of the Houthis’ political agenda, and the regional confrontation provides more leverage with which to pursue them.
The greater the Houthis’ ability to affect commercial shipping while simultaneously threatening Saudi infrastructure, the stronger their bargaining position becomes. The seizure of Mocha and the advance toward Mayyun matter are also territorial gains, since until recently the Houthi ability to shape events in the Red Sea relied mainly on missiles, drones and anti-ship systems. Geography itself is now becoming part of their military toolkit. Control of the coastline gives the movement a stronger platform from which to threaten the maritime routes upon which both Saudi Arabia and international trade depend.
Mayyun is especially important because the small island sits directly inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and divides it into two channels, making any sustained military presence there a sensitive factor for naval forces tasked with protecting commercial traffic. Control of the island would not by itself allow the Houthis to seal the international shipping route, particularly if they faced a large naval coalition. Absolute control, however, is not necessary to create a persistent atmosphere of danger. Mobile missile systems, reconnaissance assets, strike drones and unmanned surface vessels would be enough to force insurers, shipping companies and governments to account for the possibility of attack every time the regional situation deteriorates.
The experience of the Red Sea has already demonstrated how effective such a strategy can be. After Houthi attacks on commercial vessels began in late 2023, many of the world’s largest shipping companies chose to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope, on the southern end of the African continent, even though Bab el-Mandeb itself was never completely closed. Commercial shipping reacts to risk, uncertainty and rising insurance costs. The Houthis’ principal asset, therefore, is not the ability to stop every vessel passing through the strait, but the ability to make the market behave as though any vessel could potentially become a target.
Saudi Arabia comes under pressure again
The emerging situation is especially uncomfortable for Saudi Arabia, because Riyadh’s strategy in recent years has been built around gradually distancing itself from the direct war in Yemen, reducing the threat to its oil infrastructure and creating conditions in which regional conflicts would no longer obstruct the kingdom’s domestic economic transformation. A return to a large-scale campaign against the Houthis would undermine that entire approach. Saudi Arabia would once again find itself drawn into the kind of costly war it has spent years trying to leave behind through negotiations and Omani mediation. The political cost would therefore be almost as significant as the military one.
The problem becomes even more serious if instability around Hormuz forces Riyadh to rely more heavily on its East-West pipeline and Red Sea terminals. In such a scenario, growing insecurity around Bab el-Mandeb would threaten the routes intended to serve as alternatives to a vulnerable Persian Gulf. The Houthis understand this, which is why pressure on maritime traffic and the possibility of renewed strikes against Saudi energy infrastructure allow them to raise the costs for Riyadh without having to launch a full-scale offensive directly against the kingdom. What was designed as strategic redundancy for Saudi oil exports can become a second point of vulnerability.
Saudi Arabia’s response is likely to remain limited, centered on stronger air defenses, intelligence support for Ansar Allah’s Yemeni opponents, selective strikes against military targets and additional measures to secure maritime routes. At the same time, Riyadh will probably seek to preserve a negotiating channel, because the broader the confrontation between Iran and the US becomes, the more dangerous it is for Saudi Arabia to allow itself to be turned once again into one of the conflict’s principal fronts. A full return to war would expose energy infrastructure, undermine economic planning and risk once again tying the kingdom’s regional policy to an open-ended conflict in Yemen. For Riyadh, restraint is a matter of strategic self-preservation.
Washington faces a similar dilemma, because ignoring the Houthi advance risks creating the impression that American security guarantees are weakening, while a renewed large-scale operation in Yemen would require additional air, naval, intelligence and missile-defense resources at a moment when the US is already preparing for possible escalation around Iran. Even if direct war can still be avoided, the requirement to keep forces on permanent alert is itself becoming part of the price Tehran is seeking to impose on American strategy. The US is being forced to defend not one vulnerable maritime corridor but an increasingly interconnected system of routes, bases, and allied infrastructure.
A second lever is more dangerous than a second front
Neither the capture of Mocha nor a Houthi presence on Mayyun would by themselves determine the outcome of the confrontation between the US and Iran. The strategy pursued by Tehran and its partners is not built around a single decisive blow but around the gradual accumulation of risks. Washington is increasingly forced to consider the Strait of Hormuz, Bab el-Mandeb, the security of American bases, the protection of Saudi oil infrastructure, the stability of commercial shipping, and the condition of global energy markets at the same time. Each new source of tension consumes additional resources and reduces freedom of action elsewhere.
For Ansar Allah, this creates an opportunity to convert military success along the coast into political leverage, because the more expensive Red Sea security becomes for Saudi Arabia, the greater the cost to Riyadh of refusing compromises over ports, the airport, financial flows and other long-standing demands from Sanaa. For Iran, the effect is different, because Tehran gains a way to increase pressure on its adversary without deploying its own forces to a new theater and without assuming full responsibility for the geographical expansion of the conflict. The two actors benefit for different reasons, even though their immediate interests increasingly overlap.
Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are gradually becoming parts of a single system of pressure, in which a crisis at one chokepoint increases the importance of the other, while every attempt to secure one route exposes the vulnerability of its alternative. Bab el-Mandeb is not simply a second theater of war but a second political lever.

articles.title: IRGC downs third intruding US drone in 24 hours over Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
IRGC downs third intruding US drone in 24 hours over Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN — Iran’s integrated air defense network intercepted and destroyed an intruding US MQ-1 Predator unmanned aerial vehicle over the strategic Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, marking the third American drone brought down within 24 hours.
The sequence of interceptions began earlier with a successful strike by the Iranian Army’s Air Defense Forces, which brought down an MQ-1 drone in southeastern Iran. This was followed by a statement released on Tuesday morning by the Public Relations Department of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), which confirmed the downing of a second US drone by their air defense units.
These three consecutive interceptions within a 24-hour window highlight the seamless operational coordination across the country’s multi-layered defensive umbrella.
The latest interceptions come against the backdrop of heightened regional tensions triggered by US-Israeli military aggression, which has prompted Tehran to enforce strict maritime and airspace surveillance around the Strait of Hormuz—the world’s most vital energy chokepoint.
Military analysts point out that Iran’s air defense capabilities have evolved dramatically. Following US strikes on southern Iranian military and civilian sites on July 31, Iranian forces demonstrated their strategic reach by locking onto a stealth US F-35 fighter jet while simultaneously taking down an advanced MQ-9 Reaper drone.
The persistent interception of US unmanned platforms has dealt a major blow to Washington’s aerial surveillance and combat readiness in West Asia.
Reports from Western media outlets, including Bloomberg and The War Zone (TWZ), confirm that Iran’s air defense forces have neutralized more than two dozen MQ-9 Reaper drones since late February. With each unit valued at roughly 
 
 30 million, total losses for the US military have climbed past the
 
 1 billion mark, amounting to nearly 20 percent of the Pentagon’s pre-conflict Reaper inventory.
Congressional testimony reveals that the US Air Force’s active fleet of MQ-9 Reapers has plummeted to approximately 135 operational aircraft—well below the Pentagon’s mandatory minimum operational threshold of 189 platforms.
The situation is further compounded by supply shortages. General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, the manufacturer of the aircraft, confirmed that fewer than 10 new airframes remain available for acquisition, while the production line for the MQ-9A variant has been officially closed, leaving Washington with limited options to replenish its mounting losses.

articles.title: Ukraine exposes data on Russia's largest unsanctioned radio-electronics holding company
articles.body:
Ukraine exposes data on Russia's largest unsanctioned radio-electronics holding company
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has published data on companies belonging to the Concern Radio-Electronic Technologies (KRET) JSC – Russia's largest radio-electronics holding company, which supplies the Russian military-industrial complex. One-third of them are not subject to any international sanctions.
Source: DIU
Quote: "On the War&Sanctions portal, DIU publishes data on 54 Russian enterprises that are part of, or managed by, the KRET JSC of the aggressor state corporation Rostec."
Details: At present, 19 of the 54 listed enterprises are not under sanctions by any nation within the sanctions coalition.
"Adding the military-industrial complex enterprises of the aggressor state Russia to international sanctions lists, enforcing effective compliance control and ensuring inevitable punishment for violations are key to restoring peace and stability to Europe and the wider world," DIU emphasised.
The company specialises in creating electronic warfare (EW) systems, state identification systems (IFF), and onboard radio-electronic equipment for Russian fighter jets and helicopters.
Additionally, the holding company's enterprises manufacture electric motors, navigation and flight-control systems for unmanned aerial systems (UAV), anti-drone systems and remote control platforms for machine guns.
As noted by DIU, the concern also plays a crucial role in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, specifically:
- Stavropol Radio Plant Signal produces and supplies S200A1 compact jamming stations for 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles
- Kaluga Research Institute of Radio Engineering supplies 3B228 radio-electronic protection system modules for 3M22 Zircon ballistic missiles
- KRET JSC, as the parent company, directly covers funding shortfalls for state defence order contracts executed by the concern's enterprises
Among the enterprises currently not subject to sanctions are the following:
- Inertial Technologies of Technokompleks JSC, which manufactures and supplies strapdown inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2/Kh-59M2A air-to-surface missiles and Orion UAVs
- Tambov Plant Elektropribor JSC – a supplier of gyroscopic-inertial pieces for 9M727 Iskander cruise missile systems
- Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association JSC – a manufacturer of aircraft automation units, radio navigation equipment and electric motors for UAVs
Background: Recently, DIU also published data on 155 enterprises belonging to the Russian holding company Roselectronica, which manufacture components for Russian weaponry, including ballistic missiles, aviation, UAVs and EW systems. Almost half of those companies are not under any sanctions from partner nations.
Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Danish parties support government response after Russian frigate fires flares near helicopter
articles.body:
Danish political parties broadly support the government’s response after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a military helicopter Monday, according to Denmark’s Armed Forces.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats briefed party representatives Tuesday. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, to discuss the incident.
“It is completely the right thing to do,” said Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party.
The Armed Forces reported the incident in a statement at 11:02 p.m. Monday. It said an Air Force Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser.
The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
The Danish government plans to charge tourists 20 DKK per overnight stay in Copenhagen and Aarhus and introduce a levy on cruise ships, according to government sources and a memo obtained by Børsen.
The previously undisclosed measures would help fund tax cuts that the minority government will seek support for this autumn. The plans require backing from other parties, expected to come from the center-right opposition.
The government wants to abolish the 7.5% intermediate tax on annual income between 641,200 DKK and 777,900 DKK. It also plans to remove the top-top tax on income exceeding 2,592,700 DKK.
Corporate tax would fall from 22% to 19% over three years. The ceiling for share savings accounts would rise to 500,000 DKK over the same period, and taxes on shares would be reduced.
Planned funding measures include keeping the duty on chocolate and sweets, reducing the research and development deduction for companies and raising taxes on dividends received by major shareholders.
The government also wants to limit interest deductions to 150,000 DKK for individuals and 300,000 DKK for couples. Estates worth more than 10 million DKK would face a tax rate 15 percentage points higher than today.
The tax cuts are not fully covered by higher taxes and duties. The government plans to use about 1.5 billion DKK from available public funds in 2027, rising to about 2 billion DKK in 2029.
Denmark’s government consists of the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Moderates and Social Liberals. It does not have a parliamentary majority.
Danish stocks fell for an eighth consecutive trading day Tuesday as rising oil prices and interest rates weighed on the market.
At midday, the C25 index of major Danish companies was down 0.75 percent from Monday’s closing level. The index stood at about 1,845, down 70 points, or 3.7 percent, from its latest peak on September 3.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Danish bank Middelfart Sparekasse, said higher oil prices were pushing up interest rates.
Denmark’s largest companies generally carry less debt than businesses in other countries, making rising rates less of a direct problem for them, Pedersen said.
“But we cannot get around the fact that there is a risk in these rising interest rates in terms of the fact that it can drag some growth out of the economy, and that will also hit Danish companies,” he said.
Slower economic growth could reduce company revenue. Higher interest rates can also make stocks less attractive compared with bonds, which offer higher fixed returns when rates increase.
Pedersen said he did not expect an immediate major downturn in Danish shares. He described the market as strong because it has a large number of pharmaceutical and transport companies, which are less affected when consumers have less money to spend.
However, widespread selling by nervous investors would also affect Denmark because much of its stock market is owned by foreign investors.
“If everyone runs for the exit, it will also be felt in the Danish stock market,” Pedersen said. He added that such a decline would be driven more by market behavior than falling company earnings.
Denmark has rejected Russia’s claim that a Danish military helicopter acted “provocatively” before a Russian frigate fired two flares toward it Monday.
Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin said Danish helicopters had repeatedly performed “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.
“The latest incident shows that the communication problems are not on the Russian navy’s side, but on the Danish side,” Barbin wrote to the Danish news agency Ritzau.
Denmark’s Armed Forces said the frigate fired two signal or distress flares toward an Air Force Fennec helicopter in international waters off Gedser. The helicopter was conducting routine photographic monitoring of the ship.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates called Barbin’s account “a Russian excuse” and denied that Denmark had provoked the frigate.
“What we do to monitor our own immediate area is completely legal, and it does not give the Russians any alibi whatsoever to start firing at us, even if it is only with flares,” Rasmussen told Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats also said the helicopter had a legitimate reason to be there and was following normal practice.
Barbin said Russia would investigate the incident. He also cited an alleged encounter on August 27, 2025, when a Danish helicopter flew low over the Russian warship Viceadmiral Kulakov near the German island of Fehmarn.
The ambassador said that helicopter created a collision risk and failed to answer radio calls or warnings. Ritzau has asked the Danish Defense Ministry for comment on that allegation.
Denmark has summoned Barbin to the Foreign Ministry for talks about Monday’s incident.
The Danish government will require police to register all potential crimes as criminal cases and end the practice of shelving reports without a proper investigation.
The Justice Ministry announced Tuesday that it would implement all recommendations from the National Audit Office, Denmark’s independent public spending watchdog. The disputed police practice is known as “washing cases.”
“Citizens must naturally be able to have confidence that the police handle their case properly and correctly, regardless of where in the country you live,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said.
“In the future, all potential criminal cases must be registered as actual criminal cases,” he added.
The Public Accounts Committee, a parliamentary oversight body, strongly criticized police in May after receiving a National Audit Office report on the practice. Cases were reportedly shelved partly to save resources.
The new government reshuffled senior police leadership in June. Top positions in the National Police and PET, the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, changed hands.
Several justice spokespersons in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, said they had no confidence in National Police Commissioner Thorkild Fogde after he said he did not know about the practice. Fogde was later removed from the position.
The ministry did not say whether police would receive additional funding. Wammen previously said he was open to providing more money and noted that a multiyear agreement had already increased funding and training.
The National Police and Director of Public Prosecutions must regularly report on future developments to the political parties behind that agreement.
Two earlier State Prosecutor reports were not used because the National Audit Office identified issues they had missed, Wammen said.
Train services between Fredericia, Odense and Copenhagen returned to their normal schedule at 10 a.m. Tuesday after damaged overhead wires near Sorø were repaired.
Trains between Copenhagen Airport and Slagelse also resumed normal operations, Banedanmark, which manages Denmark’s rail infrastructure, and passenger rail operator DSB said on X.
Banedanmark warned that some delays could occur while services restart. It advised passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public journey-planning service, before traveling.
The damage had caused cancellations and delays since noon Monday. Repair work covered the section between Ringsted and Slagelse.
Banedanmark described the repairs as “extensive” and “very complex.” A support cable had fallen, and the equipment holding it had also been damaged.
“These are just some of the damages we see on our traction power system,” Banedanmark maintenance director Nicolai Sigsgaard said Monday.
Banedanmark received the first report of the problem at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train traffic was then stopped completely while workers identified the cause.
DSB and Banedanmark said passengers delayed by more than 30 minutes could use DSB’s travel time guarantee.
DSB paid 67 million DKK in passenger compensation during the first six months of 2026, more than twice as much as during the same period in 2025.
A delay of at least 30 minutes provides a new ticket for the same route or a refund of 50 percent of the ticket price. Passengers delayed by an hour can receive 75 percent and claim up to 75 DKK for food and drinks.
Delays exceeding 90 minutes qualify for a full ticket refund.
A 31-year-old man held in custody over an assault that led to a Swedish man’s death at a Copenhagen World Cup event will appear in court on October 7.
The hearing will begin at 1 p.m. at Copenhagen City Court, the Copenhagen Police prosecution service said Tuesday. A formal indictment has not yet been filed.
The man is suspected of punching the 32-year-old Swede hard in the jaw or neck. The case falls under Section 244 of Denmark’s Penal Code, which covers less serious violence.
The incident happened June 30 during a public screening at Islands Brygge of the World Cup match between Norway and Ivory Coast.
The Swedish man fell after being struck, hit his head and later died from his injuries. He worked for the Swedish police but attended the event as a private citizen.
The 31-year-old suspect, a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant, has been held in custody since July 3.
Two other men, ages 24 and 29, are also suspected of violence connected to the event.
The 24-year-old Danish citizen is suspected of stomping on the Swedish man while he was lying down and hitting another Swedish citizen.
The 29-year-old, a Somali citizen, is suspected of kicking the second Swedish man. Police have notified him of the charge by telephone and through his defense lawyer because they have not located him.
Police have said the three cases will be handled separately because there is no evidence that the men acted together. Court dates for the other two men have not been announced.

Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats briefed party representatives Tuesday. The Foreign Ministry has summoned Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, to discuss the incident.
“It is completely the right thing to do,” said Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party.
The Armed Forces reported the incident in a statement at 11:02 p.m. Monday. It said an Air Force Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser.
The frigate fired two flares, which are normally used as attention signals at sea. One passed close to the helicopter.
“It is obviously an escalation from the Russian side,” said Thomas Danielsen, defense spokesperson for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party.
Alex Ahrendtsen, defense spokesperson for the Danish People’s Party, urged calm.
“Of course, we should not go to war with the Russians because of some signal lights that have been sent up,” he said.
Bruus said both the frigate and helicopter had a right to operate in international waters and called the helicopter’s work normal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats described the incident as serious but unsurprising.
She said it was part of a pattern involving “an increasingly aggressive and assertive Russia” that is testing NATO and conducting hybrid warfare against Europe.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord. Our response is to stand closer together and strengthen the defence of Denmark and Europe,” Frederiksen said.
A citizen proposal seeking tighter controls on untreated wastewater discharges has received the 50,000 signatures required for consideration by the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposal, titled “Discharge of untreated wastewater into streams, watercourses, fjords and the sea,” was published September 3 and reached the threshold 10 days later, the Folketing said Tuesday.
It will now be submitted to parliament as a motion for a resolution.
The proposal contains four measures. The first would require flow meters at every wastewater overflow in Denmark. Data from the meters would be published on a digital platform, allowing the public to see how much untreated wastewater is discharged.
The second measure would require an authorized analysis company to take regular water samples and test them against 14 European Union requirements for chemical measurements.
The proposal would also introduce a fee for discharging waste substances that are diverted around treatment plants without being treated. Its final measure would require every overflow structure to have a valid permit.
The proposal received attention after Amanda Heitmann, a member of parliament for Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, signed it.
Venstre’s environmental spokesperson, Marie Bjerre, reprimanded Heitmann for supporting the citizen proposal.
“As a political party elected to the Folketing, it is not our job to sign citizen proposals, but to take a position on the content,” Bjerre told Politiken, a Danish newspaper.
Heitmann was also one of five Venstre lawmakers who recently went against the party line and voted against the fertilizer act in parliament.
Russian frigate fires flares near Danish military helicopter in international waters
A Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters off Gedser on Monday, Denmark’s Armed Forces said.
The Fennec helicopter was taking routine photographs of the ship when the flares were fired. One passed close to the aircraft, according to a military statement.
Flares are pyrotechnic devices normally used as attention signals at sea. No personnel were injured, and the helicopter was not damaged.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats called the incident serious and described Russia’s actions as “very unprofessional seamanship.”
“It is serious. It is an expression of the boundaries having been moved regarding the willingness to take risks from the Russian side,” Bruus said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen will summon the Russian ambassador to discuss the incident, though the date of the meeting has not been announced. Bruus said he did not expect further action beyond that meeting.
The defense minister said the incident would not change Denmark’s monitoring operations.
“We view it seriously, but it is not the case that we will change our behavior, understood in the sense that we have a completely legitimate task in monitoring what is going on,” Bruus said.
Inger Støjberg, leader of the Denmark Democrats, a Danish right-wing party, said the incident showed that Russian provocations had reached Denmark.
She called for NATO unity and continued support for Ukraine in its war against Russia.
“It is therefore crucial that NATO stands united, and that we continue to support Ukraine,” Støjberg said. She added that she expected a briefing from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Danish electricity prices head for most expensive month in years as gas costs rise
September could become the most expensive month for Danish electricity customers in several years, energy company Norlys said.
Halfway through the month, the average electricity price was 1.11 DKK per kilowatt-hour in western Denmark and 1.12 DKK in eastern Denmark.
It is the first time since December 2022 that the monthly average has exceeded 1 DKK per kilowatt-hour, according to Norlys.
“We are halfway through September, so a lot can still change, but with the rising gas prices, we unfortunately have to expect that it will be an expensive month,” said Ellen Trolle, director of Norlys’ energy business.
Electricity prices were set to rise above 7 DKK per kilowatt-hour Monday evening, their highest level in almost two years.
Norlys said the increase was caused by higher gas prices and limited electricity production from wind and solar power. Natural gas plants often supply electricity when the weather does not provide enough wind and sunlight, making power prices more sensitive to gas costs.
Kristian Rune Poulsen, an analyst at Danish energy organization Green Power Denmark, also pointed to gas prices.
“The conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, which doesn’t really want to come to an end, means that a great deal of the liquefied natural gas that we have become so dependent on cannot get out onto the world market,” he said.
Poulsen said prices would continue to fluctuate but were unlikely to fall soon while the conflict continued.
“We expect that the elevated price level will persist throughout the winter, as it looks right now,” he said.
Nearly 12 percent of Danish ninth graders fail to pass Danish or mathematics exams
More than one in 10 Danish ninth-grade students failed to earn a passing grade in Danish or mathematics in this summer’s final exams, new government figures show.
The Ministry of Education said 11.8 percent of students did not receive at least 2, the minimum passing grade, in one or both subjects during the 2025-2026 school year.
“It is too high a proportion. Because it means that they initially will not have the opportunity to move on to youth education programs,” Andreas Rasch-Christensen, a school researcher at VIA University College, a Danish higher education institution, told DR, Denmark’s public broadcaster.
DR reported a failure rate of 10.5 percent, while the ministry listed 11.8 percent. The difference is that the ministry included students whose schools did not register that they sat the exam. DR excluded those students.
The result marks a small decline from the previous school year, when 9.9 percent failed to pass Danish or mathematics. The rate was 10.1 percent in 2023-2024 and 6.9 percent in 2018-2019.
The average final exam grade was 7.3, in line with the previous four years, DR reported.
The figures follow the release of a PISA study showing that Danish students’ performance had declined in reading, mathematics and science.
The government said similar declines were occurring across much of Western Europe. Danish politicians have pointed to mobile phones as a possible cause, saying quick stimulation from phones may make it harder for students to concentrate.
The government wants to introduce a complete ban on mobile phones in schools.
Lower food VAT would cost Danish businesses about 725 million DKK a year to administer
Lowering Denmark’s value-added tax on food would cost businesses about 725 million DKK annually in added administration, according to a parliamentary response.
Tax Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates said Monday that the government wants to lower the general VAT rate on food and remove it from fruit and vegetables as soon as possible. The changes will not take effect this year.
“It is of great importance to the government to make it cheaper for Danes to fill their shopping baskets,” Engel-Schmidt said at a consultation.
The estimate is uncertain because the government has not decided how the new VAT system would work. Shops and other businesses would have to cover the administrative costs.
Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry and Denmark’s main business and employers’ association, said the actual cost would be higher.
“When the VAT rules for food become more complicated, it affects the VAT accounting in virtually all active businesses,” tax policy chief Jacob Bræstrup said.
Bræstrup said the change would affect more than wholesalers, supermarkets and restaurants. He said total administrative costs would be “significantly higher” than the estimated 725 million DKK.
The broader proposal would cost the state 17.4 billion DKK a year, according to the Ministry of Taxation and Growth.
Leading economists have criticized the plan as an expensive and inefficient way to help people. They warn that businesses might not pass the full tax reduction on through lower prices. Some savings could instead pay for administration or increase company earnings.
The government plans to present several possible models in the second half of 2026.
Extensive damage to the overhead wire system near Sorø is expected to disrupt train services between Ringsted and Slagelse until 10 a.m. Tuesday, according to Banedanmark, which manages work on Denmark’s rail network.
One track has reopened after DSB, the Danish passenger train operator, stopped services on the section around midday Monday. Trains are now running on a reduced timetable, with longer travel times and some cancellations.
Tony Bispeskov, DSB’s head of information, said priority would be given to international, InterCityLyn and InterCity trains.
Banedanmark said it received a report of problems with the overhead wire system between Sorø and Slagelse at 12:45 p.m. Monday. Train services were stopped completely while the cause was identified.
“There we can see that we have extensive damage to one of our tracks. At the moment, this means that we only have one passable track to operate on, and that we are running with a reduced timetable,” Banedanmark said.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said Monday that she is “quite optimistic” Denmark, Greenland and the USA can reach an agreement on security and defense in Greenland.
Frederiksen spoke at a news conference in Finland, where she attended a European summit focused on security in the Arctic.
“We have agreed to start a high-level working group on closer cooperation on security and defense, also in Greenland,” Frederiksen said.
“As long as the working group between Greenland, Denmark, and the USA continues its work, it is too early to draw a conclusion. But I am quite optimistic that we will succeed in finding a way,” she said.
Frederiksen visited Greenland last week with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Denmark is among 10 NATO countries conducting a joint military exercise in Greenland. The exercise is intended to show that Denmark and NATO are protecting Greenland and the Arctic.
US President Donald Trump has criticized Denmark for not doing enough to protect Greenland from threats posed by Russia and China.
During the first weeks of September, 400 soldiers from 10 NATO countries are operating on land, at sea and in the air near Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq. They are training to operate in Arctic conditions as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry surveillance and deterrence mission.
“If one is to be able to operate in the Arctic, one has to train up here,” Søren Andersen, head of Denmark’s Arctic Command, told the Danish news agency Ritzau last week.
Andersen said the temporary Arctic Shield exercise is part of a long-term strategy for Greenland and the Arctic.
“For us, it is about helping to transform NATO’s northern flank into a hard target. Meaning all the way from Alaska across Canada, Greenland, and to the northern part of Norway,” he said.
Denmark and Greenland are also discussing whether to give the USA greater access to Greenland. The New York Times reported in the spring, based on American sources, that the USA wants three bases in Greenland as part of a possible agreement. Narsarsuaq and Kangerlussuaq were reportedly among the possible locations.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats declined to discuss the working group’s talks during a visit to Narsarsuaq last week.
“I cannot comment on that. What goes on in that working group, goes on in that working group,” Bruus told Ritzau.
Bruus said the government wants to extend the operating period of Narsarsuaq Airport by one year if it receives support from the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Initially, it is a one-year extension. That gives us the opportunity to extend the playing board,” Bruus said.
Chief of Defense Michael Hyldgaard said Narsarsuaq would be an obvious possible location for an American base because of its position in southern Greenland and its access to transatlantic routes, the Denmark Strait and the GIUK gap.
The GIUK gap is the sea area between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom. It is an important military passage where NATO can monitor and block Russian submarines moving toward the Atlantic.
The USA previously operated a military base in Narsarsuaq from July 1941 to November 1958.
CPH Half will expand to 45,000 runners for its race on September 19, 2027, because of high demand, organizer Sparta Atletik og Løb, a Danish athletics and running organization, said in a news release.
Around 35,000 people are taking part in this year’s half marathon, up from about 32,000 in 2025.
Tickets for the 2027 race will be sold through a lottery instead of on a first-come, first-served basis.
Registration for the lottery opens September 16 and remains open for two weeks. People can register alone or in groups of up to three. Each group will either be selected together or not selected at all.
Selected runners will have 48 hours to buy a ticket. The price is DKK 795 plus a small administration fee.
“When demand is so high, access to the bib numbers must also function in a way where everyone has a fair and equal chance of getting a bib number,” Dorte Vibjerg, CEO of Sparta Atletik og Løb, said in the release.
The organizers also used a lottery to sell tickets for this year’s CPH Half, which is part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships. Similar systems are used for major marathons in Berlin and London.
This year’s race starts Sunday. Elite international runners will begin first, followed by the other participants.
Danish police brought 79 new charges linked to possible crime-for-hire cases from January through the end of July, the Ministry of Justice said Monday.
In total, police brought 316 charges from April 2024 through the end of July this year that may involve crime-for-hire, a practice also known as “Violence as a Service.”
The figures come from NSK, a Danish police unit that handles serious and organized crime. In January, authorities had recorded 237 charges, according to figures released by the ministry in February.
The government disclosed the latest figures as it sent a bill proposing stricter penalties and other measures against gangs and crime-for-hire for consultation. That process allows judges, lawyers, police and other groups to submit concerns or objections before the proposal moves forward.
The bill would increase penalties for crime-for-hire and treat criminal families in the same way as gangs.
“We will not tolerate children and young people being recruited into a life of crime, and residential areas being marked by fear, control, and parallel power structures,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said in a statement.
The proposal would also add a provision to the penal code intended to make it easier to convict people who provide minor services to gang leaders.
Other measures include allowing background checks for dockworkers and increasing the penalty for violating a stay ban. Police have recorded a large increase in such violations.
A stay ban can be imposed on a person who has committed a crime connected to a gang. It prevents that person from entering a specific area, such as part of a town or municipality, for a set period.
Violating a stay ban currently carries a fine of 10,000 DKK. Under the proposed law, a violation would result in 30 days in prison.
Power and diesel prices heading for nearly two-year high

According to Troels Skipper, commercial director at OK, the high electricity price is due to a combination of rising gas prices and a lack of wind and solar energy.
“Right now, we are in the unfortunate situation where the high gas price pushes the electricity price up along with it. And unfortunately, we do not get enough electricity production from wind turbines and solar cells to push the price the other way,” he said.
The last time the hourly price was at around seven DKK per kilowatt-hour was in December 2024.
Also, Diesel prices in Denmark rose to a record high on Monday, reaching 19.19 kroner per litre after an increase of 20 øre, according to FDM, the Danish motorists’ association. Petrol prices also increased by 40 øre per litre. FDM consumer economist Ilyas Dogru said the increases followed the weekend’s escalation in the war involving the United States, Iran and Israel.
Denmark is set for a week of changing autumn weather, with periods of rain, sunshine and mild temperatures, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, DMI.
Monday began cool, particularly in central Jutland, where temperatures fell to between 6 and 8 degrees.
“The temperature is down to 6-8 degrees, so if you are going out cycling, you can clearly feel that autumn has arrived,” DMI duty meteorologist Jesper Eriksen told Ritzau.
The rest of Monday is expected to remain dry, with a mix of sunshine and clouds. Temperatures will reach between 15 and 18 degrees, with light to moderate winds from the west.
### Tuesday to be warmest day
Tuesday is expected to be the warmest day of the week.
Winds will turn to the south, bringing slightly warmer air over Denmark and pushing temperatures to between 17 and 21 degrees.
There will be periods of sunshine, although some rain is possible, particularly in Jutland.
More rain is expected to reach Jutland later Tuesday afternoon before moving east during the evening and overnight.
Wednesday will bring some sunshine but also showers.
Temperatures are expected to fall back to between 15 and 18 degrees, while winds will turn west again.
Thursday and Friday are expected to bring periods of rain and showers, with temperatures remaining between 15 and 18 degrees.
Winds from the west and southwest are also expected to strengthen gradually toward the end of the week.
Eriksen said the week would not be particularly cold despite the unsettled weather.
“In the week as a whole, you will not need the really warm clothes, but in periods you will need rainwear and rubber boots,” he said.
It remains unclear whether September will bring another spell of warmer weather later in the month.
“We will have to see what happens, whether the last spasms with some warmth arrive. It is not decided yet,” Eriksen said.
More than half of the Danish schools that were selected for the latest Pisa survey declined to participate. In total, 398 schools were drawn for the survey. Of those, 215 chose not to participate, writes Kristeligt Dagblad.
When a selected school chooses to decline, a reserve school could step in. In advance, two reserve schools had been designated for each of the drawn schools.
Therefore, a total of 283 schools ended up participating in the survey. However, this is significantly fewer than in 2022, when 347 schools participated.
According to Kristeligt Dagblad, the number also remains below the OECD’s “technical minimum requirement”.
According to Monika Klingsbjerg-Besrechel, chief consultant at Statistics Denmark, which was responsible for the practical part of the survey, the many declines have not affected the quality of the survey.
“Fortunately, we reached a higher response rate, but despite that, we were unfortunately still below the minimum requirement from the OECD. If we had not had the reserve schools, we really would have been in serious trouble,” she says to Kristeligt Dagblad.
She points out that it was subsequently investigated whether the many declines had affected the result.
Silkeborg debuts as first host city for Royal Run 2027
Danmarks Idrætsforbund (DIF) has announced Silkeborg as the first of five host cities for the 2027 edition of the Royal Run, making it the first time the Central Jutland city is on the bill for the event.
“I am wildly happy about the news that we will be a host city for Royal Run in 2027, and I am looking forward very much to welcoming a public celebration in running shoes right in the middle of Silkeborg,” said the city’s mayor, Helle Gade.
Thus, the run moves to the city that also brands itself under the name ‘Denmark’s Outdoor Capital’, something the mayor looks forward to showcasing.
“Here in Søhøjlandet we have a unique setting for both participants and spectators with hilly landscapes, great viewpoints over the Silkeborg lakes, and an exciting city center where urban life and nature merge. I look forward to showcasing that.”
In 2026, the host cities were Randers, Ringkøbing, Middelfart, Helsingør, and Copenhagen/Frederiksberg. This year, Denmark can expect new cities other than Silkeborg to join the Royal Run host club, with a new host city scheduled to be announced every day this week.
The Royal Run offers three distances to run, including 1.6 kilometers (also known as one mile), five kilometers, and ten kilometers.
The event first took place in 2018, when the then Crown Prince turned 50 years old. Since then, it has been held every year on Whit Monday.
Last year, a record 112,450 runners participated.

articles.title: Ukraine successfully tests interceptor against faster Gerans as Russia floods its skies with drones
articles.body:
Ukraine has successfully tested another interceptor designed to counter Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Geran attack drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 15 September.
The test comes as Russia rapidly expands the use of faster jet-powered Gerans, creating a new problem for Ukraine’s air defenses: these drones give defenders less time to detect and engage them while allowing Russia to maintain large-scale attacks. A successful interceptor could give Ukraine a cheaper, scalable way to counter that threat without relying as heavily on scarce high-end air-defense missiles.
Zelenskyy said Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi reported the successful test, during which the new interceptor struck a Russian Geran drone.
The system still reportedly needs further work, including improvements to some aspects of its control. But the successful test marks another step in Ukraine’s effort to develop a new layer of air defenses against Russia’s faster drones.
Russia is making its drone attacks faster and larger
Russia has sharply expanded its use of jet-powered Gerans in recent months, adding a faster and more difficult-to-intercept threat to its large-scale drone campaign.
Geran is Russia’s designation for its domestically produced Shahed-derived attack drones, with newer jet-powered variants representing a major upgrade over the earlier propeller-driven models.
Zelenskyy recently said Russia launched around 2,100 drones against Ukraine last week, alongside nearly 1,700 guided aerial bombs and 78 missiles. The attacks have increasingly targeted energy facilities, railway infrastructure, businesses, and residential areas.
The newer Gerans are faster than earlier Shahed-derived drones and can reach targets deep inside Ukraine. Their speed gives Ukrainian air defenses less time to detect, track, and engage them.
Russia has also changed how it uses its drones. Rather than concentrating attacks almost exclusively overnight, Russian forces have increasingly launched waves during the day as well, keeping Ukrainian cities under repeated air-raid alerts.
The result is a growing challenge not only of interception, but of scale. Ukraine must defend a large territory against increasingly large drone barrages while preserving more sophisticated air-defense missiles for ballistic missiles and other threats.
Ukraine is building a new layer of air defense
Ukraine has already been racing to develop such systems. In late August, Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said four potential interceptor systems capable of shooting down jet-powered Gerans had undergone field testing. Ukraine was aiming to bring them to the required level and eventually produce thousands of units.
Today’s announcement shows that effort continues to produce concrete results.
Ukraine is also expanding other parts of its counter-drone network. Zelenskyy said the country is increasing purchases of electronic warfare equipment and reorganizing mobile fire groups and air-defense positions.
The goal is to build enough layers to cope with Russia’s evolving drone campaign: electronic warfare, mobile fire teams, traditional air defenses, and increasingly specialized interceptors.
Russia is making its drones faster and launching them at greater scale. Ukraine’s response is now moving beyond adapting existing defenses toward developing weapons specifically designed to catch them.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Refinery, Aircraft Plant and Ozon Facility in Massive Overnight Attack
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces launched a massive drone and missile attack on several Russian regions early Tuesday morning, Sept. 15, hitting a Rosneft-owned oil refinery in the Samara region and other industrial facilities.
The Samara region was targeted by more than 40 drones, according to regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Damage was sustained by one of the industrial facilities as well as several residential buildings,” he wrote on Telegram, adding that there were no casualties.
According to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+, the Rosneft-owned Syzran Oil Refinery was among the targets.
The facility has an annual crude oil processing capacity of about 8.5 million tons and produces approximately 800,000 tons of gasoline and 1.5 million tons of diesel fuel annually.
Following the attack, storage tanks containing petroleum products caught fire at the facility. The refinery was previously struck by drones on Aug. 4.
Later, the General Staff of Ukraine confirmed the strike on the Syzran Oil Refinery.
“Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck the Syzran Oil Refinery (JSC) in Russia’s Samara region and the ‘Atlant Aero’ facility in Taganrog, Rostov region.”
An impact followed by a fire was recorded at the Syzran Oil Refinery. The AVT-6 primary oil processing unit and the tank farm were hit, the report states.
The plant produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, as well as other petroleum products. The facility supplies the needs of the Russian armed forces, the General Staff added.
Intel Reveals 19 Russian Missile, Drone Firms Still Outside International Sanctions
Russian facilities reportedly hit
In the Rostov Oblast, a massive missile attack resulted in “multiple impacts on the ground” and several fires, Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar reported.
According to Slyusar, two apartment buildings and three private homes, an educational institution, commercial buildings, agricultural warehouses, a grocery store and an Ozon logistics center were damaged.
“Preliminary information indicates there are no fatalities or injuries,” Slyusar wrote.
Exilenova+ also reported that the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific-Technical Complex was among the targets of the missile strike.
The Beriev TANTK aircraft plant in Taganrog is a key Russian aircraft repair and maintenance facility. OSINT analysts reported that Russian military aircraft were undergoing repairs there at the time of the strike, although the specific types and number of aircraft could not be independently confirmed.
Later, the General Staff clarified that explosions and a fire were recorded at the “Atlant Aero” facility, although earlier reports indicated that the Beriev plant had been hit.
“Atlant Aero” specializes in the manufacture of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and their components. Specifically, the enterprise produces “Molniya” strike-reconnaissance UAVs and components for “Orion” UAVs.
The company is involved in meeting the Russian armed forces’ requirements for unmanned systems, the General Staff added.
Strikes come amid energy truce talks
The attack came amid uncertainty over a proposed agreement to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump recently said that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv was prepared to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if its partners could guarantee that Russia would also stop attacking Ukraine’s energy sector. He emphasized that any such agreement would need to be reliable and long-lasting.
However, according to sources cited by the Financial Times (FT), Russian President Vladimir Putin is unwilling to agree to a mutual halt to strikes on energy infrastructure before winter.
The sources said Putin believes continued attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector could increase pressure on Kyiv and force it to make concessions.
At the same time, sources told the publication that Moscow and Kyiv have resumed negotiations over a possible halt to strikes on energy facilities, although no final agreement has been reached.
In a morning update on Telegram, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia continues its strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector, logistics networks and critical infrastructure.
“And our responses to them are significant. There are new results from Ukraine’s Defense Forces regarding the oil refinery in Syzran; there were also hits on a drone manufacturing plant in Taganrog and a drone training and launch site in the Oryol region.”

articles.title: After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on Britain
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on Britain on the world stage
UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced a wide-ranging ban on the sale of products produced in Israeli settlements, and on financing and business activities there. He did so in concert with France and Canada, which strengthened the impact of the new policy. They acted in response to a government campaign to terrorise Palestinian inhabitants of the West Bank.
Over 60 villages with almost 5,000 inhabitants have been entirely depopulated. At least 1,100 have been killed by armed settlers and IDF soldiers who not only protect them, but participate directly in the attacks.
An import ban on goods from illegal settlements and a new ban on arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation” were among the measures announced. A comprehensive sanctions regime against services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK, as well as personal sanctions against the main individuals accused of promoting settler violence, were also included.
Israel lobby
Israel’s political leadership reacted with fury to the sanctions. In August, Netanyahu had declared bizarrely that “the first Islamic Republic to have nuclear weapons will be the Islamic Republic of Britain.” He further retaliated by closing the country’s East Jerusalem consulate and placing ten Labour MPs on a travel ban list. Curiously, the foreign secretary was omitted, as were other government ministers, including PM Andy Burnham, who publicly supported the new policy.
The Board of Deputies and chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis released statements accusing Labour of anti-Semitism. This is ironic considering Miliband is a child of Holocaust survivors, who came to Britain as displaced persons after WWII.
Among the lobby’s claims is that the new policy will “make Jews less safe.” This is a mantra repeated whenever Israel faces anti-genocide measures. Mirvis added they would embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews.”
In fact, defending Israeli crimes as the Lobby does actually endangers Jews, because it gives the impression that supporting such behaviour is intrinsic to Judaism itself.
The Israel Lobby demands condemnations over the settlement ban while saying nothing about Israel’s mass murder of nearly 75,000 Palestinians in Gaza and thousands more in attacks on Lebanon and Iran. Since 10/7, two British Jews have been killed in an attack on a synagogue.
The Board of Deputies linked the government’s measures to the High Holidays, claiming it would put Jews in jeopardy from anti-Semitic attacks against their synagogues on Rosh Hashanah. They even argued that the Labour government was putting the “party’s interests” above those of “the nation.”
This too is an attempt to dismiss the moral element of the new policy. Labour instituted it not because it offers a political advantage, but because it honours international humanitarian law and upholds rulings of courts of justice.
Zionists (and white supremacists) deliberately conflate Jews with Zionism. Thus they exploit the universal condemnation of anti-Semitism for the purpose of tainting efforts to hold Israel accountable for its crimes, including the Gaza genocide, and wars of aggression in Syria, Lebanon and Iran.
The Argentina distraction
In a search for anything that might damage the UK government, far-right ministers like Itamar Ben Gvir, dredged up Argentina’s long-dormant Falklands claim. They are encouraging Argentina to revive its right to sovereignty in the hopes of stirring up an international controversy that might embroil the UK.
The Israeli minister wrote in a Spanish-language post on X: “It's time for the State of Israel to publicly recognise that the Malvinas Islands are Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently stole from the Argentine people.”
Ben Gvir is also aware that, as the police minister responsible for the torture and murder of Palestinian prisoners, he has been banned by multiple countries. In response to the government’s recent action, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada announced new sanctions on Ben Gvir and Betzalel Smotrich.
It seems the Israeli far-right doesn’t recognise the irony of linking Argentina seeking the return of its territory from a colonial power to Israel’s colonising of Palestine.
It couldn’t be clearer that the Malvinas dispute is an apt metaphor for Israel’s occupation of Palestine and usurpation of Palestinian national rights. What is Israel doing if not occupying the Palestinian people and appropriating its natural resources?
Just as “it’s time to recognise that the Malvinas are Argentine,” it’s time for the world to recognise that Palestine is for Palestinians, and it has been “violently stolen” from them.
Unprecedented settlement ban and sanctions regime
While foreign governments have made gestures of protest, including scores of nations recognising Palestinian statehood, the new measures mark the first time Western governments have taken such a stance.
Recognising a Palestinian state was a symbolic political act with low cost; just as the suspension of arms shipments to Israel during the worst of the genocide was temporary and soon lifted. All of these had little economic or reputational impact.
The settlement ban imposes real (though limited) economic costs on Israel. It restricts global markets for settlement products and shuts off foreign financing for their projects. More importantly, Miliband’s new foreign policy legitimises such sanctions for other nations, which will undoubtedly follow suit.
Nevertheless, the settlement ban has limitations. In fact, British diplomats told the Trump administration that the measures were largely cosmetic. Bloomberg reported that British diplomats have privately told the US the sanctions are largely symbolic and will have no material impact on the UK’s wider relationship with Israel on trade or security, in a bid to soothe the Trump administration’s response.
In addition, these sanctions will have limited practical impact. The UK exports $8 billion in trade to Israel. It has not broken down that figure to isolate trade with settlements. Thus, it is difficult to know how it will enforce the ban. Britain imports only $6 million worth of Israeli goods. So any prohibition on these products would have minimal impact.
The Israeli state vs. Israeli people
The foreign secretary suggested that the government’s anti-settlement plan targets the Israeli government rather than the Israeli people. However, polls show this distinction should no longer hold.
The majority of Israelis serve in an occupation army responsible for these crimes, and most don’t raise their voice against the mass murder and expulsions by settler terrorists in the West Bank.
Israelis are also clearly voting for parties that not only support such an approach but also devise and enact it. This is the work of the entire state of Israel: its government and its people.
Another inadequacy of the new policy is that it targets a relatively small sector of the Israeli public and economy. It will not punish the country in any substantive way. Furthermore, the settlements are only one element in the regime of oppression which Israel has inflicted on the Palestinian people. It will not address the genocide in Gaza, apartheid or ethnic cleansing. It will not restrain Israel’s wars of aggression, which are riling the entire region.
There must be sanctions that impact Israel’s entire economy, including ending military aid, joint weapons development with Israeli arms makers, and severing diplomatic relations. Britain must campaign for fellow members of the UN Security Council and its European allies, in a united front. They, in turn, must enact real, punishing sanctions that will shock Israelis into the realisation that they are no longer welcome at the table of nations.
In what appears to be a diplomatic non sequitur, in order to make the settlement policy less controversial, Miliband has declared new sanctions on Iran and Hezbollah. These punishing measures impose actual harm on Iranians and Lebanese, unlike the settlement policy.
It’s interesting that the measures against Israel captured the world’s attention, while having limited impact, whereas those against Iran and Hezbollah will have real impact and are rarely, if at all, reported by the media.
Richard Silverstein writes the Tikun Olam blog and is a freelance journalist specialising in exposing secrets of the Israeli national security state. He campaigns against opacity and the negative impact of Israeli military censorship.

articles.title: Kremlin blasts US move to militarize space
articles.body:
Kremlin blasts US move to militarize space
Weapons should not be deployed in space, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said, responding to the Pentagon’s announcement that the US has placed a weapons system in orbit.
US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink disclosed the deployment on Monday, saying the US Space Force “now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action,” without providing details about the system. Media reports have suggested that it is intended to disable or destroy hostile satellites.
“We believe that space should be free from any weapons. And certainly we count on broad international consolidation… to continue efforts for the full demilitarization of space,” Peskov told journalists on Tuesday during a regular briefing.
The Pentagon has a long history of using orbital systems for military purposes, specifically intelligence gathering, navigation and communications. Some US military concepts, however, have also envisioned systems potentially capable of conducting strikes from space. During the Cold War, for example, the Soviet Union viewed the Space Shuttle as a potential platform for delivering a rapid nuclear strike.
Countries regarded by Washington as strategic rivals, including Russia and China, have reportedly developed anti-satellite capabilities that could deny the US the advantage in space during a direct conflict. The use of such weapons, however, could produce significant unintended consequences.
The so-called Kessler effect describes a scenario in which collisions generate increasing amounts of orbital debris, triggering further collisions and potentially making low Earth orbits unusable for an extended period.
Russia has long called for stronger international agreements restricting the military use of space. While the Outer Space Treaty prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction in orbit, Moscow has argued that conventional weapons should also be banned.
In June, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz announced that his country was developing a space-based anti-satellite laser system and aimed to become “the leading country in the world with this capability.”

articles.title: Pentagon report puts Iran war cost at $33.4 billion, cites US weapons shortfalls and extensive base
articles.body:
Pentagon report puts Iran war cost at $33.4 billion, cites US weapons shortfalls and extensive base
TEHRAN- A newly released US government report has shed further light on the financial and military costs of Washington’s war with Iran, estimating that the conflict had cost the United States $33.4 billion by June 29, while Iranian strikes damaged or destroyed hundreds of structures and dozens of American aircraft across US military facilities in the Middle East.
The figures are contained in the latest Lead Inspector General report to Congress, issued by the US Department of Defense and covering the conflict through the end of June. The assessment highlights not only the scale of material damage sustained by US forces but also mounting pressure on American weapons stockpiles and the defense-industrial base responsible for replenishing them.
Billions spent as US munitions stocks come under pressure
According to the report, $22.3 billion of the $33.4 billion total was spent on munitions, while equipment losses accounted for another $3.7 billion and other expenses for approximately $7.4 billion. The heavy consumption of American weapons during the campaign, the report said, “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
The assessment is significant because the United States entered the conflict with one of the world’s largest and most sophisticated military arsenals, yet the pace of weapons expenditure exposed limitations in its ability to rapidly replenish key systems during a sustained high-intensity conflict.
The report also puts the direct physical damage to US diplomatic facilities in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates at $184 million because of Iranian attacks. Separate emergency response and evacuation operations added substantially to the overall cost of the conflict.
The findings contrast with repeated assurances from US President Donald Trump that American weapons production remains exceptionally strong. Ahead of the report’s release, Trump said the United States was producing more “Exquisite and Elite Weapons” than at any point in its history.
Iranian strikes damage US aircraft and military infrastructure
The Pentagon assessment also documents the impact of Iranian attacks on US military installations across the region. Hundreds of buildings and other structures were damaged or destroyed, while dozens of aircraft were lost or damaged by the end of June.
Among the aircraft affected was an F-35A Lightning II, which sustained damage from Iranian fire. The incident was particularly notable because it represented the first reported combat damage to an F-35A, one of the most advanced and expensive aircraft in the US inventory.
The report also recorded the destruction of four F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and one A-10 Thunderbolt II, while seven KC-135 Stratotanker aerial-refueling aircraft were damaged or destroyed. In addition, seven helicopters and more than 30 unmanned aircraft were lost.
Earlier Congressional Research Service assessments had already identified at least 42 US aircraft lost or damaged during Operation Epic Fury, although the CRS cautioned that its figures were based on publicly available information and could be revised as additional information emerged. 
 
 Continuing losses underline the cost of the campaign
The military costs have continued to accumulate beyond the period covered by the Pentagon report. In early September, an Iranian ballistic-missile attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan damaged an A-10 and approximately eight F-15 aircraft, according to US officials. The A-10 reportedly suffered severe damage to one wing, while the F-15s were assessed as serviceable after sustaining lighter damage.
The attack also required US forces to launch roughly 30 Patriot interceptors, adding to concerns over the availability of expensive air-defense munitions. Reuters reported that US officials and analysts have warned of pressure on interceptor inventories after months of sustained operations.
The emerging picture is therefore one of a conflict imposing costs well beyond the battlefield itself. In addition to the billions of dollars spent on combat operations, the United States has faced damage to bases and aircraft, depletion of high-value munitions and growing demands on its defense-industrial supply chain.
For Washington, the report offers a rare official accounting of the price of the Iran war and highlights a central challenge of prolonged high-intensity warfare: maintaining the pace of weapons consumption while simultaneously replacing sophisticated systems that are costly, technologically complex, and difficult to produce at scale.

articles.title: Ukraine Reports 219 Frontline Clashes as Fighting Intensifies Near Pokrovsk
articles.body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported 219 combat engagements along the frontline by 10 p.m. local time on Tuesday, Sept. 15, with the most intensive attacks being concentrated on the Pokrovsk axis.
According to the daily evening update, covering the previous 24 hours of fighting, Russian forces carried out 68 airstrikes, dropped 249 guided aerial bombs (KABs), used 4,153 loitering munitions and shelled Ukrainian positions and populated areas at least 1,638 times during the day.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“A total of 38 attacks were repelled on the Pokrovsk axis,” the General Staff said, describing fighting near 17 settlements, including Dobropillia, Udachne and Molodetske.
Heaviest fighting near Pokrovsk
According to the AFU, Russian troops attempted to advance near Sofiivka, Pryiut, Kucheriv Yar, Vilne, Nove Shakhove, Stepy, Hannivka, Novyi Donbas, Dobropillia, Bilytske, Vodiane, Krasnopillia, Novofedorivka, Vasylivka, Serhiivka, Udachne, and Molodetske.
The preliminary figures indicated that 66 Russian servicemen were killed and five wounded in the sector.
Twelve vehicles, one artillery system, five pieces of specialized equipment, a drone control point, two ammunition depots, and 45 Russian shelters were destroyed.
Additionally, three vehicles, three artillery systems, one piece of specialized equipment, eight drone-control points, and 101 Russian shelters were damaged.
The AFU destroyed or suppressed at least 147 Russian drones of various types.
Drone Crash Near Strategic German Airbase – Another Failed Sabotage Attack?
Frontline fighting
On the South Slobozhanskyi axis, Russian forces launched 15 assaults near Lyman, Prylipka, Starytsia, Izbytske, and Mala Vovcha, with one clash still ongoing at the time of the report.
The AFU repelled two Russian attacks near Kivsharivka and Tabaivka on the Kupiansk axis, while another combat engagement continued.
Six Russian attempts to advance were also repelled on the Lyman axis near Novoselivka, Drobyshcheve, Stavky, Lyman, and Dibrova, where one clash was still underway.
According to the General Staff, four Russian attacks were stopped near Ozerne, Kryva Luka, and Mykolaivka on the Sloviansk axis, with one assault reported near Yurkivka on the Kramatorsk axis.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, the AFU repelled eight Russian assaults near Kostiantynivka and Illinivka, and toward Osykove, Mykolaypillia, and Novohryhorivka.
Four engagements remained ongoing at the time of the report.
Southern axes
The General Staff reported one Russian attack near Verbove on the Oleksandrivka axis and seven attacks near Hirke and Charivne on the Huliaipole axis.
On the Orikhiv axis, the AFU repelled one Russian assault near Zarichne.
No activity was reported on the North Slobozhanskyi, Kursk, or Prydniprovske axes.
No significant changes were recorded elsewhere along the front either, the General Staff said.
