articles.title: Russian regions report Ukrainian strikes as Rostov governor cites 'massive' missile attack
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Ukrainian missile and drone strikes hit several Russian regions early Tuesday, with Kyiv confirming attacks on an oil refinery and a drone production plant as Russian authorities reported damage to residential, industrial and commercial sites.
Rostov Governor Yury Slyusar said the region was subjected to a “massive missile attack,” with damage reported in the city of Taganrog.
An educational institution, commercial building, gas pipeline, agricultural warehouses, grocery store and Ozon warehouse were damaged, Slyusar said on Telegram. Taganrog Mayor Svetlana Kambaeva said five apartment buildings were also damaged, but reported no casualties.
Reports also indicated damage near the Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex, although the extent and circumstances were not immediately confirmed by regional authorities.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Atlant Aero plant in Taganrog, which it said manufactures drones.
In the Samara region, more than 40 drones were shot down overnight, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. An industrial facility and several residential buildings were damaged, but no deaths were reported, he added.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck the Syzran oil refinery, reporting a fire and damage to a crude oil distillation unit and storage tanks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also confirmed strikes on the Syzran refinery and a drone production facility in Taganrog. He said Ukrainian forces had also struck a drone preparation and launch site in the Oryol region and targets in the Black Sea.
In the Voronezh region, Governor Alexander Gusev said the attack damaged windows at a municipal building as well as the roofs and facades of four private houses. No casualties were reported, he said.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out group strikes with attack drones on logistics centers and ports in Ukraine, as well as vessels it said were used by the Ukrainian armed forces.
In the Odesa region, the ministry said a logistics center used to store and distribute military cargo arriving in Ukraine from abroad was hit in the settlement of Velyka Balka.
At the port of Chornomorsk, a dry cargo vessel and a ferry that the ministry said had delivered cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it added.
Russian forces also continued strikes on railway infrastructure in western Ukraine used to transport military cargo from European countries, the ministry said.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia cancels oil shipments to Europe after pipeline attack – Reuters
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia cancels oil shipments to Europe after pipeline attack – Reuters
Saudi Arabia has cancelled some oil shipments to Europe after drone attacks forced the shutdown of its key East-West pipeline, Reuters reported on Tuesday, adding to mounting pressure on global crude supplies as instability threatens energy infrastructure across the Middle East and North Africa.
Riyadh reportedly informed European customers that some crude cargoes scheduled for loading later in September will be cancelled, while loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu have been suspended, oil trading and shipping sources told the news agency. Saudi Aramco declined to comment.
The disruption follows drone attacks that damaged the East-West pipeline, which crosses Saudi Arabia from its main oil-producing areas in the east to Yanbu on the Red Sea. Riyadh has blamed the strikes on an Iraqi militia.
The route had become particularly important over the past six months because it allowed Saudi crude to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been severely disrupted by the conflict with Iran. Its loss leaves Riyadh increasingly dependent on exports through the Gulf at a time when normal tanker traffic through Hormuz remains constrained.
According to Reuters, traders expect Saudi Arabia to attempt to move more crude through the strait using so-called dark shipments similar to those employed by the United Arab Emirates and Iraq. Such shipments have allowed Gulf producers to export an estimated 7 million to 9 million barrels per day, equivalent to around 30% to 40% of pre-war volumes, according to shipping data.
The tightening supply picture has already pushed up prices. Brent futures were trading near $108 a barrel on Tuesday, while physical cargoes in Europe were substantially more expensive, with benchmark dated Brent at around $122 a barrel, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.
Poland is among the countries facing immediate pressure. State-controlled refiner Orlen is rushing to secure replacement cargoes from the North Sea and other suppliers, according to five industry sources cited by Reuters. Saudi Aramco became Orlen’s largest crude supplier in 2022 and now provides around 40% of its oil, helping Poland end its reliance on Russian crude but leaving it heavily exposed to disruptions in Saudi supplies.
The pressure on Saudi export infrastructure comes amid renewed fighting with Yemen’s Houthis. The group has launched ballistic missiles and drones at targets inside the kingdom, while Saudi Arabia has resumed airstrikes in Yemen. Saudi authorities said 13 civilians were injured in attacks on Khamis Mushait, Abha and Taif on Monday.
Air raid alerts have also been activated across southern Saudi Arabia amid fears of further attacks. The risk is particularly acute around Jizan, which hosts major Saudi energy infrastructure, including a large oil refinery.
The escalation is simultaneously putting pressure on the Red Sea route itself. The Houthis have expanded their position along Yemen’s western coast and seized strategic territory near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, through which vessels must pass when traveling between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
The emerging squeeze leaves Saudi Arabia facing risks on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula: Hormuz remains severely disrupted to the east, while the infrastructure and shipping routes used to bypass it are increasingly exposed to attacks in the west.
The problem could be particularly acute for Europe, which is simultaneously facing another supply disruption in Libya.
Libya’s National Oil Corporation (NOC) said on Tuesday that production and operations had been halted at the Hamada and Al-Tahara fields and the NC5 station after members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard forcibly closed a valve on the main Hamada-Zawiya pipeline. The closure triggered a sudden pressure increase at the Tahara connection point and forced all three sites offline.
The NOC warned that it could declare force majeure if the valve remains closed or if forced shutdowns spread to other fields, saying prolonged disruptions would damage Libya’s economy and its reputation as a reliable energy supplier.

articles.title: Gas Stations Hit, Explosions Rock Kyiv as Russia Launches 200-Drone Attack
articles.body:
Russian forces attacked Kyiv with drones early Tuesday, Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least seven others, while UAV strikes and falling debris damaged buildings and gas stations across the capital, according to Ukrainian officials.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) announced an air raid alert at 5:25 a.m.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
At the same time, the Ukrainian Air Force tracked jet-powered drones entering the Kyiv region and heading toward the capital before subsequently appearing over the city itself.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv at approximately 5:34 a.m. and again at 5:42 a.m.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko later reported on Telegram that a Russian drone had struck a gas station in the city’s Darnytskyi district, injuring one person.
“Medics hospitalized one wounded person. The man is in critical condition,” he wrote.
He also said that, according to preliminary information, a warehouse facility in the Obolonskyi district had been hit.
A drone threat was announced in Kyiv again at 7:49 a.m. At around 8 a.m., Kyiv Post reporters heard a very loud explosion.
Klitschko subsequently confirmed that a UAV had apparently struck a non-residential area in the Solomianskyi district.
“Emergency services are en route to the scene,” he added.
In an 8:51 a.m. report, Klitschko said heavy smoke was reported in the Holosiivskyi district following a drone strike on a gas station.
NATO Jets Shoot Down Drone Over Lithuania
“Two people have already been wounded in the morning attack on the capital. Medics have hospitalized both of the wounded,” the mayor said.
Klitschko later clarified that the number of casualties had risen to four. All four are being treated in city hospitals, with two in critical condition.
The State Emergency Service (DSNS) later reported that eight people in Kyiv had been injured by Russian strikes since the start of the day.
“Solomianskyi district: a non-residential building was hit; no fire broke out. Six people were injured,” the report said.
Rescuers also confirmed that a gas station in the Darnytskyi district had been hit, injuring one person. The resulting fire was minor and was extinguished with fire extinguishers.
“Holosiivskyi district: a strike occurred at a gas station. One person was injured. The fire has been extinguished. Obolonskyi district: a non-residential building caught fire. Firefighters have brought the blaze under control,” the DSNS added.
In a 10:35 a.m. report, Klitschko announced that one of the people injured in the morning attack on the capital had died in hospital.
“The man had been hospitalized in critical condition,” he added.
187 drones downed or suppressed
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 200 strike UAVs against Ukraine starting at 6 p.m. on Sept. 14. The attack included Shahed-type drones, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerbera and “Parodiya” (Parody) decoy drones.
The attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
“According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m., air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 187 enemy UAVs,” the Air Force said.
Russian drones were recorded striking seven locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three other sites.
This story will be updated as new details become available.

articles.title: Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
Poland scrambled fighter jets overnight on September 15 in response to renewed Russian attacks on western Ukraine involving jet-powered strike drones, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command reported.
At around 4 a.m., the Operational Command said Polish and allied aircraft had been deployed as Russian jet-powered drones carried out strikes against targets in Ukraine. Ground-based air defense and radar systems were also placed on heightened readiness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The measures were taken as a precaution to protect Polish airspace and “aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions.”
At around 6:30 a.m., the Operational Command announced that the potential threat had passed and that the forces and systems activated during the alert were returning to standard operational status.
“No violations of Polish airspace were recorded,” the Operational Command said.
The heightened readiness in Poland came as NATO responded to another aerial incident elsewhere on its eastern flank. Earlier the same night, NATO aircraft intercepted and destroyed an unidentified drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, with preliminary information indicating that it had arrived from Belarus, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
The drone crossed into Lithuania shortly after midnight, triggering air alerts in several areas. About 30 minutes later, NATO fighter jets operating from the Šiauliai Air Base intercepted and shot down the aircraft over the Kaunas region.
Lithuania’s military said Italian fighter jets carried out the interception. The drone’s wreckage was subsequently found in a rural area, where police cordoned off and secured the site.
The incidents follow another recent airspace breach involving a NATO member. On September 8, Romania deployed two F-18 fighter jets after military radar detected an aerial object entering Romanian airspace at around 4:47 p.m., roughly 18 kilometers north of Roman.
The detection prompted air raid warnings in several nearby communities. Shortly beforehand, at approximately 4:20 p.m., neighboring Moldova reported that a drone, preliminarily identified as a Shahed, had entered its territory.

articles.title: Zelensky’s political endgame has begun
articles.body:
Zelensky’s political endgame has begun
Although Ukrainian authorities have rejected any idea of unity between the peoples of Russia and Ukraine, the best metaphor for their country’s modern political system is a traditional Slavic winter game called ‘King of the Mountain’. In this game, any player who manages to reach the so-called ‘mountain’ (dominating height) must defend it at all costs against rivals. When another player knocks off the ‘king of the mountain’, he takes his place until the next ‘king’ topples him, and so on.
Much like in this children’s game, leaders have quickly succeeded one another in modern-day Ukraine – in fact, former President of Ukraine Leonid Kuchma (the first to promote the state concept “Ukraine is not Russia”) was the only Ukrainian leader to serve two consecutive presidential terms. Today, there is no democratically elected head of state: Vladimir Zelensky’s term ended in 2024.
Since then, Zelensky has invested all of his political capital into suspending elections, which for him would mean ‘political suicide’. Apparently, Ukraine’s political system has ceased to disguise itself as a democracy, as was the case in 2004, when an unconstitutional third round of elections was held to secure Victor Yushchenko’s victory; now, however, there is nothing but a ruthless struggle for power in the country. In this uncompromising fight, which disregards the genuine aspirations of the Ukrainian people, the reigning ‘king of the mountain’ exercises authority not for the good of the nation but rather to eliminate any potential ‘contenders’ who threaten the established status quo.
Road to the ‘mountain’
In this context, it’s hard to accuse Zelensky of political opportunism; he knows better than anyone in Ukrainian politics how to storm the heights of power. Born in the city of Krivoy Rog, Zelensky long sought to conquer another Olympus: Moscow, the former capital of the once-unified USSR. However, he encountered setbacks, like failing to be admitted to the Moscow State Institute of International Relations (an alma mater of many Russian officials and leaders of post-Soviet countries).
His team was defeated in the KVN semifinals, and had a falling out with the show’s host, Aleksandr Maslyakov, who had turned the post-Soviet comedy sketch contest into a mass cultural phenomenon and an important tool of Russia’s soft power. Then, Zelensky’s Studio Kvartal-95 was gradually pushed out of the Russian entertainment industry.
All this forced the enterprising young man to carve his own path in Kiev. Zelensky’s big opportunity came in the latter half of the 2010s with the release of the TV series ‘The Servant of the People’. It told the story of a modest high school teacher who was elected president after his video exposing Ukraine’s corruption issues went viral. In real life, Zelensky, who had skillfully crafted an image of a ‘Ukrainian Ronald Reagan’ from the earliest days of his presidential campaign, rose to power by means of skillful criticism of his predecessor, Pyotr Poroshenko, and promises of peace in Donbass.
However, even before the start of Russia’s military operation aimed at demilitarizing and denazifying Ukraine and protecting Donbass, it became clear that Zelensky’s election promises would remain unfulfilled. Following the start of the war, he consciously missed opportunities to resolve the conflict at earlier stages – such as during the April 2022 talks in Istanbul.
Protecting the dominating height
Today, Ukraine’s political discourse revolves around the possibility of presidential elections, which Zelensky would likely lose due to war fatigue and valid concerns about Ukraine’s approach to negotiations with Russia. As Moscow adopts a harder stance following each round of negotiations, Ukrainians have justifiably begun to question the price paid for fighting “to the last Ukrainian,” especially since the final terms of settlement become less favorable as time passes.
Zelensky’s main rivals will attempt to hold his team accountable for the lost territories, the devastated economy, and the depletion of the nation’s population. At the same time, they will push the narrative that Zelensky’s policies were not merely misguided but effectively criminal, driven by a desire for self-enrichment. These are the reasons behind the series of anti-corruption investigations involving Zelensky’s inner circle, including figures like co-owner of Studio Kvartal 95 Timur Mindich, and former head of Zelensky’s office Andrey Yermak.
Against this backdrop, there has been a notable surge in activity among those vying for Zelensky’s position. Valery Zaluzhny, the former Commander-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces and presently Ukraine’s Ambassador to the UK, is by now a familiar figure with seemingly limited chances for victory.
However, the emergence of Mikhail Fyodorov in the upper echelons of Ukrainian politics has become the biggest sensation of the year and triggered the biggest political crisis during Zelensky’s presidency. Born in the village of Vasilyevka in Zaporozhye region (now part of Russia), 35-year-old Fyodorov gained recognition when he became Minister of Digital Transformation and later Minister of Defense. He proposed high-tech methods for waging war against Russia – views that clashed with those of then-Commander-in-Chief of the AFU Aleksandr Syrsky.
Sensing a threat to his own power from the young, up-and-coming politician, Zelensky reshuffled his cabinet and dismissed both Fyodorov and Syrsky. The seemingly unjustified removal of a minister who enjoyed unprecedented popularity among Western media sparked a wave of civil unrest in several Ukrainian cities and was dubbed the “Cardboard Maidan.”
Despite Fyodorov’s appointment as advisor to the Italian Minister of Defense and the rapid decline of protests in Ukrainian cities, this episode is now rightly regarded as the most significant domestic political challenge for Zelensky since 2019, and is perceived by many analysts as a final warning ahead of a potential power transition.
The King’s fall is coming
This is particularly relevant when viewed in the context of US President Donald Trump’s recent uptick in diplomatic activity. Facing the risk of losing the fragile Republican majority in Congress following November’s midterm elections due to his failed operation against Iran – one that not only paralyzed the Strait of Hormuz and exposed the limits of American influence in the Middle East but also triggered a severe energy crisis leading to soaring fuel prices in the US – the Trump administration, in need of a resounding foreign policy success, has decided to return to resolving the Ukraine crisis. Despite repeated claims by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio about the demise of the “Spirit of Anchorage”, the US has made several attempts to revive negotiations.
This included CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s discreet visit to Moscow, followed by talks between US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent and his counterpart, Russian Minister of Finance Anton Siluanov, on the sidelines of the G20 summit. Most recently, US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made visits to Moscow and Kiev. So far, the most tangible outcome of these diplomatic efforts has been the announcement of a resumption of trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US set for October, immediately after the Russian legislative elections. So what does Trump’s renewed activity around Ukraine mean for Kiev?
The Anchorage agreements may have indeed become less relevant; however, this should not be seen as a testament to the effectiveness of Ukrainian diplomacy in bringing Trump back into the realm of “Euro-Atlantic solidarity.” Rather, it may signal a looming shift at the front: the Russian Armed Forces are close to liberating the Slavyansk-Kramatorsk urban agglomeration.
As we may recall, Zelensky’s refusal to withdraw Ukrainian forces from the remaining areas under Kiev’s control in Donetsk region was a key sticking point that prevented the implementation of the “Anchorage Formula.” The loss of Donbass – especially in light of Russia’s effective strikes against Ukrainian port infrastructure that have essentially cut off Ukraine’s access to the Black Sea – places Zelensky’s regime on the brink of collapse. Consequently, there is a strong likelihood that a final settlement agreement will be signed by a new “yellow-blue king of the mountain”...

articles.title: Chinese drones over German bases, paid saboteurs lighting fires for Russia—Germany’s military spells out the new normal
articles.body:
Russia has made Germany a priority espionage target, and the threat from cheap, deniable sabotage carried out by civilians paid for one-off jobs is rising, Germany's Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD) said in its 2025 annual report—the first published under a new law obliging annual disclosure. MAD blamed Germany's geostrategic position in Europe and NATO, the expansion of the Bundeswehr, and the introduction of new weapons systems. Repeated sabotage cases on German soil last year were "with high probability" Russian-run, MAD said.
For two years Berlin has publicly warned about a Kremlin campaign of arson, surveillance, and drone incursions run through cheap local proxies—mostly at press briefings and closed sessions. A January 2026 transparency law now forces that warning onto the statutory public record, sharpening the burden of an operational answer. Germany hosts NATO's logistics spine for arming Ukraine—the very hub Moscow's proxies keep aiming at.
Sabotage on the cheap
"Hybrid attacks have increased in Germany," MAD said.
The threat from "low-level agents"—residents paid small sums to plant fires or photograph military sites—has significantly increased. Recent incidents match the model: a bomb-laden drone found in August beside a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport was traced this month to a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal, and two Bulgarian nationals were arrested over a September suspected arson near defense-electronics firm Rohde & Schwarz in Munich. Russia's Legalresidenturen — intelligence outposts inside embassies, semi-state bodies, and press agencies—remain a central instrument of Moscow's information-gathering.
A masked figure got into a Polish drone-parts plant—Poland now suspects a foreign spy service set the fire
Chinese drones over bases, blackmail risk for soldiers
Some drone overflights and unauthorized entries at Bundeswehr sites are attributable to Chinese intelligence, MAD said, which is also drawing on parts of the Chinese diaspora in Germany.
The service flagged travel by German soldiers to Russia and Belarus: personnel with family ties there kept visiting despite the security climate, drawing the attention of Russian and Belarusian intelligence services and creating particular exposure to blackmail and threats.

articles.title: Lithuania briefs EU allies after drone shot down by Nato jets overnight – Europe live
articles.body:
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
A drone shot down in Lithuania last night was carrying an explosive device, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas said (15:32).
The drone crossed into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus (13:05) and was downed near a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant in Kruonis, minister confirmed.
The drone was shot down by Italian fighter jets operating as part of a Nato mission (10:25), with the Italian defence minister saying it “most probably” came down from Russia (14:33).
Meanwhile,
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador to Copenhagen after a Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish army’s helicopter in the Baltic Sea in the latest of incidents attributed to Moscow (9:58).
Russia denied responsibility for the incident, blaming Denmark (12:25, 12:45).
The EU (15:07) and Ukraine (12:37) offered their support to Denmark.
Separately,
The Dutch authorities are investigating who could be behind a series of suspected sabotage attacks that disrupted the operation of its railways, including on a number key transport routes across the country (10:03, 11:40, 13:26).
The final results of the Swedish parliamentary election are now not expected before Thursday, with a higher-than-usual number of votes yet to be counted (10:30).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
'Russia manipulates and blames Denmark' but 'demonstrates its intention to escalate' after helicopter incident, EU defence commissioner says
Meanwhile, EU defence commissioner Andrius Kibilius condemned Russian attempts to “manipulate” about the helicopter incident and “blame Denmark.”
Indirectly responding to Russian comments earlier today (12:25, 12:45), he said:
“Russia manipulates&blames Denmark.I have full trust in [Danish] words&evidence. Russia demonstrates its intention to escalate. Russia needs to know: hybrid attacks against Europe will be met [with a] strong&united European hybrid defence!”
Germany searches for debris after drone crashes near military airbase
Separately, German authorities are searching for debris from a drone believed to have crashed near Lake Steinhude in the Hanover region, just one kilometre from the German Bundeswehr’s airbase in Wunstorf, Bild reported.
The tabloid said some parts of the drone have already been found, but investigators hope to recover more “to rule out potential threat” and track down who is behind it.
Regional broadcaster NDR reported that the debris was found on Monday, and there is no further threat to the public.
“Further information can only be released after the search and any findings have been examined,” authorities were quoted as saying.
'These are not isolated incidents,' EU's von der Leyen warns
The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen condemned “reckless and dangerous Russian behaviour.”
She saidthe events in Denmark and Lithuania were “not isolated incidents,” but “part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe, testing our readiness and our resolve.”
“Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger. We are reinforcing our collective deterrence and defence, together with Nato. And we are stepping up the pressure on Russia,” she said.
Italy has decided to extend for another 15 days the suspension of the European Union’s Schengenborder-free arrangement with Spain, Reuters reports Rome’s interior ministry said on Tuesday.
Italy names Russia as probable source of drone shot down over Lithuania
The Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto has said that the drone shot down by an Italian Nato fighter over Lithuania “most probably” came from Russia.
The downed drone fell in a rural area near Lake Kaunas, in the centre of the country. Lithuania’s defence minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Nato allies had been informed about the incident and discussions were under way. A presidential security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said the drone may have strayed off course.
Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all of which are Nato members and share a border with Russia – have regularly reported drone incursions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. A Nato fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Tuesday there was no viable parliamentary majority in Germany outside his coalition with the Social Democrats (SPD).
Dismissing the prospect of a minority government, Reuters reports Merz said “I was elected for four years and want to use this time to solve problems,” adding that he hoped to agree on further reforms with the SPD after upcoming state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
After the AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt, observers are closely watching those elections for more signs of faltering public support in Merz’s policies.
A Ukrainian army unit has launched a counteroffensive against Russian forces near Lyman, an embattled town in Ukraine’s east, AFP reports the unit’s commander said Tuesday.
The area has been the site of intense battles throughout the four-and-a-half-year war.
“The 3rd Army Corps has launched an offensive operation called Vivaldi in this sector,” the commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, Andriy Biletsky, said in a video on Telegram.
It was reported that Ukrainian troops had made a small pocket of gains north of the town, whose capture could pave the way for Moscow’s forces to sweep south and threaten the Ukrainian-held Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
Dutch railway tracks disrupted by sabotage in 30 locations, operator says, as King opens new parliament session
Let’s catch up on the situation in the Netherlands (10:03, 11:40).
In the latest update, the track operator Pro Rail has said that various pipes and other items were found at 30 locations across the country.
All trains in the vicinity of the track blockages were halted, while there were also serious disruptions elsewhere, including to international services to Germany, Reuters reported.
In some cases, there were also cases of new blockages re-appearing in the same places after they were cleared, NOS reported.
The incident comes on Prinsjesdag, or the Prince’s Day, when King Willem-Alexander formally opens a new session of parliament and sets out the government’s plans for the 2027 budget.
Lithuania to send a note to Belarus about drone incursion as investigation continues, minister says
Meanwhile, Lithuanian foreign minister Kęstutis Budrys said that Lithuania will deliver a note to Belarus to set out what it knows about the overnight drone incursion into its airspace.
He added that the work to determine the type and ownership of the drone was underway. “We will take other actions based on that,” he said in comments quoted by Lithuanian broadcaster LRT.
Budrys added that Nato’s eastern flank “must be strengthened and its resilience increased” amid growing tensions with Russia.
Helicopter incident between Russia and Denmark reflects rising tensions, expert says
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
Experts said that Monday’s incident on the Danish straits reflects increasing tensions between Denmark and Russia that is slowly moving towards Cold War levels.
Ebsen Salling Larsen, a military analyst at the Center for Joint Operations at the Danish Defence Academy, said it is normal for Danish ships, helicopters or planes to go out to monitor Russian state-owned ships and warships. Sometimes this prompts Russian crew to point weapons at them or use a tracking radar.
But Monday’s incident, during which Russian flares were fired at a Danish helicopter, was unusual and marked a “change in pattern”.
“There’s an ongoing tension and the incident yesterday talks to that increased tension somewhat,” said Salling Larsen. “If you go back to the cold war you have more incidents of ships bumping into each other and so forth. We are slowly reaching that level again.”
The show of force, he said, was a reaction to Danish support for Ukraine and the Baltic states.
It is unlikely that Denmark would close the Danish straits, he said, because Copenhagen wants to follow international law and has its own vested interests in being able to move freely.
“That would be a Pandora’s box we would rather not open,” he said. “We are a small state with a large merchant fleet so we have some interests there as well.”
Russian frigate issued no warning or attempted radio contact before firing flares at Danish helicopter, minister says
Meanwhile, Denmark’s defence minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters that no warning or radio contact was made before a Russian frigate fired flares towards a Danish military helicopter.
He also said the flare from the frigate passed “within a matter of meters” from the Danish helicopter.
Bruus said it showed Russia’s increased willingness to take risks in its aggressive behaviour.
Russia's ambassador blames Denmark for helicopter incident
After speaking to the Russian media (12:25), Moscow’s ambassador to Copenhagen Vladimir Barbin was somewhat more incendiary in his comments to the Danish media.
He told Danish broadcaster DR that essentially it was the Danish helicopter that provoked the Russian ship, branding it a “reckless” behaviour.
He also accused Denmark of showing “no interest … in preventing the situation from escalating.”

articles.title: NATO jets down drone over Lithuania as Russian ship fires flares at Danish helicopter
articles.body:
NATO jets down drone over Lithuania as Russian ship fires flares at Danish helicopter
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace and Denmark accused a Russian frigate of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter on Tuesday, in incidents that heightened tensions along the alliance’s eastern flank.
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight, officials said Tuesday, the day after the head of the alliance said strikes close to its territory would only increase its support for Ukraine in the war against Russia's full-scale invasion.
Military officials in Lithuania, a NATO member, said the incident marked the first time that a drone had been shot down in its airspace. Authorities didn’t comment on the drone’s origin or purpose, saying further investigation was needed, but two senior officials said the device was likely carrying explosives.
Read moreUkraine war live: NATO downs drone over Lithuania
Officials in other NATO countries, including Germany, Denmark, the United Kingdom and Poland, have in recent weeks accused Russia of involvement in acts such as drone incursions, sabotage, arson and surveillance of defence facilities and in plans to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport.
Separately, Denmark said Tuesday that one of its air force helicopters was fired on with flares as it was carrying out surveillance of a Russian frigate in the Baltic Sea.
Strikes close to NATO territory showed Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror”, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday. He spoke after a Russian drone struck a railway line near the Ukraine-Poland border on Sunday shortly after senior visiting officials passed through.
Rutte pledged to bolster the 32-nation alliance's own defences along its long eastern border with Russia and with Belarus, a Russian ally.
Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Commission, said the incidents in Lithuania and Denmark were not isolated but “part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe, testing our readiness and our resolve”.
“Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger,” she said.
The drone downed Tuesday in Lithuania fell near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles (100 kilometres) west of the capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas Reservoir, Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center said Tuesday.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the crisis centre, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the drone most likely entered from Belarus. It remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and flew along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted, he said.
Writing on Facebook on Tuesday, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said an explosive device was detected on the drone and neutralized by bomb-disposal experts.
Menacing drones have repeatedly loomed over the skies of Lithuania, which shares borders with Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
Read more'A fight for your way of life’: Lithuania's culture minister on Ukraine and Russian disinformation
In May, residents of Vilnius were told to take shelter, and the president and prime minister were taken to safe locations during an alarm over drone activity near the border with Belarus.
Stray Ukrainian drones have also previously crossed the border into Baltic airspace, including in May, when a NATO fighter jet shot down a Ukrainian drone over southern Estonia.
Meanwhile, Denmark accused Russia of firing flares at one of its air force helicopters in connection with “routine photographic coverage” of a Russian frigate in waters off the port of Gedser in the Baltic Sea.
“This is completely unacceptable,” the Danish foreign ministry wrote on X, saying that the Russian ambassador was summoned over the incident.
Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, said it was “not the first time” that Danish air force helicopters “carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships”.
He said the Danish helicopter conducted “provocative actions against the Russian frigate”.
The Kremlin declined to comment Tuesday, with presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying that he did not have details.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

articles.title: Iran dismisses US talks possibilities over Trump mixed messaging
articles.body:
A to Iranian official ruled out Tuesday any talks with the United States after President Donald Trump said he was open to resuming discussions on the Middle East war.
"Don't get distracted by the U.S. president's mixed signals – from 'no negotiations' to 'we're ready to talk,'" the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, posted on X.
"The stakes around oil and the straits have changed. Damage control won't stop what's coming. No talks until Iran's conditions are met. Period!" he added.
Earlier Monday, Trump said he was open to holding talks with Iran, after weeks of saying it was too early to make a deal to end the war.
"The failing Nation of Iran wants to make a deal, quickly and badly. I will determine whether or not the U.S.A. will choose to engage – The concept of which we are open to," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Iran has repeatedly listed demands including war reparations and the lifting of sanctions as preconditions for ending the war and its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
Meanwhile, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed Tuesday that it intercepted and "destroyed" two MQ-1 drones were near the Strait of Hormuz, marking the fourth such drone it says it has downed in recent days.
The IRGC said the drone was shot down east of the waterway by a newly deployed advanced air defense system operated by its Aerospace Force under Iran's integrated air defense network.
The Guards added that it intercepted another MQ-1 drone west of the Strait of Hormuz, without providing details on its operator or the exact location of the incident.
On Monday, they had also claimed to have "destroyed" another drone of the same type, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB.
In a separate development, Iran's Armed Forces General Staff issued a nationwide passive defense directive outlining preparations for three possible scenarios: the end of war, a cease-fire and full-scale war.
Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, chief of staff of the Iranian Armed Forces and chairman of the country's Permanent Passive Defense Committee, issued the 10-article directive for Iran's 2026 Passive Defense Commemoration programs, according to Fars News Agency Tuesday.
Under the full-scale war scenario, large public gatherings and in-person events would be suspended, with activities instead focusing on operational preparedness, continuity of essential services, resource management, public assistance and coordination among relevant agencies.
In the event of a ceasefire without a definitive end to hostilities, the directive prioritizes public preparedness, vigilance against hybrid warfare and information security, while the end-of-war scenario provides for the full implementation of planned exercises, training and public programs.
The directive also calls for operational plans to be updated based on experiences from what it describes as Iran's "second and third imposed wars."
Iran has issued similar directives for its annual Passive Defense Commemoration in previous years, including 10-article instructions in 2024 and 2025 focusing on public preparedness and protecting critical infrastructure.
The latest directive, however, comes amid the ongoing war with the U.S. and explicitly sets out measures for three different conflict scenarios.
The U.S. and Israel launched large-scale attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, targeting government buildings, military sites, missile infrastructure, and air defenses. Iran responded with missile and drone attacks against Israel and U.S. bases across the region.
The conflict has since expanded across the region, while diplomatic efforts have sought to end the hostilities.
Before the current conflict, Iran and Israel had also fought a 12-day war in June 2025, which ended with a U.S.-backed cease-fire.

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine ready for 'de-escalatory steps'
articles.body:
Ukranian President Volodymyr Zelensky (AFP Photo)
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that Ukraine is ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the U.S. leader announced on Sept. 14 that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his nightly address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure.”
He added: “If this can become the first de-escalatory step, stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response, then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation.”
Zelensky said “we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia’s war economy.”
He noted that “so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the war.”
“But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps.”
Trump has insisted that the Russia-Ukraine war, and not the conflict with Iran, was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November.
A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the U.S.-Israeli conflict against Iran, now in its seventh month. U.S. envoys went to Moscow and Kiev earlier this month without announcing a breakthrough.
While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelensky has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defenses as Russia intensifies its attacks.
Russian strikes on Ukraine’s rail network are worsening each week, the CEO of the state Ukrainian Railways operator told AFP on Sept. 14, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend.
“It’s growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one,” said Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
European Union countries on Sept. 14 delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist, diplomats said.
An EU list of almost 3,000 individuals and entities, which needs to be extended every six months, was set to expire by Sept. 16.
However, ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition, the diplomats said.
The Financial Times reported, quoting people familiar with the issue, that France was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving French citizens held in Azerbaijan.

articles.title: BAE Unveils Cheap, Compact Electronic Warfare Systems for Small Platforms
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—BAE Systems is building a new slate of compact electronic warfare tools for small airborne platforms that could coordinate with fighters, work with helicopters, or augment legacy aircraft with outdated, hard-to-update EW suites.
The “Shadow EW” family will be produced out of the company’s Cedar Rapids, Iowa, facility, said Josh Niedzwiecki, vice president and general manager of electronic combat solutions for BAE.
The company announced the new systems here Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Niedzwiecki couldn’t share details on specific platforms that Shadow might work with, but he did say the devices can perform standalone EW functions and can both complement and augment existing EW systems.
“If you’re on a platform and now you have another sensor or networked set of sensors in the environment that are providing spatially differentiated information about the battlespace that can be communicated back to, say, a manned platform, then it allows you to have a better picture, and then make better decisions,” Niedzwiecki said.
The “family” of Shadow systems include the 100, 120, and 500.
The Shadow EW 100 is designed for smaller platforms, mostly drones or attritable systems. It operates in the wideband radio frequency range of 70 MHz–6.0 GHz.
The Shadow EW 120 specializes in radar EW while also conducting signals and communications intelligence. It works in 
5 MHz–6.0 GHz RF coverage.
The Shadow EW 500 can do edge processing and is built for Weapons Open System Architecture platforms. It works in the 10 MHz-18 GHz RF coverage.
While much has been made of the Air Force’s push to boost production of kinetic munitions—from the cheap Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program to existing air-to-air systems to new hypersonic weapons—the service is also looking for cheaper ways to deliver nonkinetic effects, such as electronic warfare.
Small Package
With the Shadow EW systems, BAE is looking to be “ahead of need” for the Air Force, anticipating that the service will want readily available EW tools.
David “Kooler” Krumm, BAE’s VP of business development and a retired USAF three-star, said the service will likely need such systems particularly for systems that require more work and funding to upgrade.
“Some of our legacy systems are just older and a take longer time [to upgrade]. Having something that you can carry now, use it to have the effect of an electromagnetic spectrum that you want, allows you to expand your capabilities across the board,” Krumm said. “So, it’s a very quick way to respond to emerging threats.”
BAE decided to take a “low-cost … high volume” approach to Shadow to respond to what Krumm said is an operational need for more EW arrows in the quiver.
The company is “working through” the price point for the EW packages, but while many sophisticated EW suites on board U.S. Air Force aircraft can cost several million dollars each, Niedzwiecki said Shadow will cost between thousands and tens to hundreds of dollars, depending on the features provided.
Without sharing specifics, Niedzwiecki said BAE is targeting active Pentagon programs with Shadow EW.
“The short answer is in the electronic warfare segment of our business, building ahead of need is usually very aligned to a very specific contract where we know something’s coming and we’re going to get ahead to make sure we buy material ahead of time to a contract,” Niedzwiecki said.
The smaller, cheaper option also lets operators deploy EW effects without giving away their position.
“Every time you communicate and radiate in the battle space, you’re also vulnerable. And so, if you can not have to rely on other assets to tell you where things are, then you have a much better chance of getting a target,” Niedzwiecki said.
The devices are also field programmable, which bypasses lengthy installation-level software updates or upgrade work.

articles.title: Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy truce. Neither side stopped the strikes.
articles.body:
Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy truce. Neither side stopped the strikes.
Russia and Ukraine kept trading strikes just hours after U.S. President Donald Trump claimed the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire.
Ukrainian forces attacked Rosneft’s Syzran oil refinery in Samara region in the early hours of September 15, sparking a fire at the plant. More than 40 drones were shot down over the region overnight. In Taganrog, the strikes damaged warehouses belonging to Ozon and local agricultural businesses, along with an educational institution, a store, and several residential buildings. The independent Telegram channel Astra reported that the Taganrog-Tsentralny military airfield was also hit. No casualties were reported in either Taganrog or Samara region.
Russian drones struck Kyiv the same morning. The strikes set two gas stations ablaze in the city’s Darnytskyi and Holosiivskyi districts, injuring eight people. A warehouse and several nonresidential buildings elsewhere in Kyiv were also hit. In Zaporizhzhia, a strike on an infrastructure facility killed one man and injured four other people.
“Russia is not stopping its strikes on our energy sector, everyday logistics, and critical infrastructure. And our responses to that are tangible,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote this morning.
Hours earlier, Trump had said on Truth Social that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop striking energy facilities, claiming that Russia’s war against Ukraine — not the U.S. war with Iran — was driving the rise in diesel prices.
The Financial Times called the statement premature. The paper reported that the idea of an energy ceasefire had already been discussed — first at trilateral meetings between the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine, and then, after those talks collapsed in February, through separate contacts and back channels. But sources told the newspaper that Putin does not want such an agreement before winter: Moscow is counting on strikes against Ukraine’s energy system during the cold season to ratchet up pressure on Kyiv and force it into concessions.
Two senior Ukrainian officials told the FT that Trump’s statement was intended to show voters his administration is working to lower fuel prices. It was not the first time Trump had blamed Ukraine for high diesel prices: on the evening of September 13, he directly urged Zelensky to stop striking refineries that produce diesel, saying it is “hurting the world.”
Retail diesel prices in the U.S. have hit a record $6 per gallon (about 3.8 liters) — a problem especially acute for the Trump administration ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
A source familiar with the U.S. delegation’s recent talks with Putin in Moscow confirmed to Agentstvo that no ceasefire decisions were made during those talks, and that Trump’s announcement was an “improvisation.”
After the morning attacks, the Kremlin stated that it was aware of the ceasefire idea and supported it, but that simply halting strikes on refineries would not solve the problem of high global prices. According to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, doing so would first require ensuring the safe seaborne export of petroleum products and lifting sanctions on Russian energy supplies.
War in photographs: the aftermath of Russian drone strikes on gas stations in Kyiv.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: NATO country could cease to exist in days if it attacks Russia – Putin aide
articles.body:
NATO country could cease to exist in days if it attacks Russia – Putin aide
Poland could cease to exist as a state within days if it enters a war against Russia, Nikolay Patrushev, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, has warned in response to Warsaw’s claims that NATO could quickly defeat the country.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said over the weekend that Poland and its allies would enjoy overwhelming air superiority in a hypothetical conflict with Russia.
“If Russia attacked us and we took our gloves off, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly,” Sikorski claimed at the Yalta European Strategy meeting in Kiev, adding that NATO could destroy Russia’s oil refining capacity within six weeks.
Patrushev dismissed the assessment as an “amateurish view” of Russia’s military might, pointing out that Moscow isn’t utilizing its full military potential in the Ukraine conflict.
“If Poland were to enter military action against Russia, our country would employ the full arsenal of its available forces and resources, and Polish statehood would cease to exist within two or three days,” he said in an interview given to Russian media on Tuesday.
Patrushev also accused Sikorski of “Russophobic” militarism, forgetting the lessons of history, and of repeatedly endangering his own country rather than ensuring its security.
Other Russian officials have also condemned the Polish minister’s rhetoric. Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Grushko said Sikorski’s calls for NATO to conduct more aggressive exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region should be assessed by “people in white coats,” while Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described his comments as “Russophobia of the brain.”
Warsaw, along with the Baltic states, Germany, and other European countries, have increasingly claimed that Russia could eventually attack NATO territory and have called for increased military spending and a stronger presence of the bloc along Russia’s borders.
NATO has also discussed strengthening its nuclear posture in Europe, with Washington reportedly considering stationing US strategic weapons in Poland and the Baltics.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it intends to attack any NATO members, describing related suggestions as fearmongering used to justify militarization. Even Poland’s own defense minister said in July that there was no indication Russia was preparing a full-scale attack on the country.
Russian officials have instead warned that Europe’s accelerating rearmament and increasingly aggressive military planning are themselves raising the risk of a direct confrontation.
Putin recently noted that Western states are now openly talking about preparing for war with Russia, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has stressed that Moscow has “no reason” to attack Europe unless it is attacked first.

articles.title: Italian jets destroyed a drone over Lithuania in the first such shootdown in the country
articles.body:
NATO fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania shortly after midnight on 15 September, the first time alliance aircraft have destroyed one over that country, LRT reported. The aircraft crossed in from Belarus and came down near a village in the center of the country, where military police sealed the site. Its type and operator have not been established.
What happened over Lithuania
Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center issued a yellow air alert after midnight, first for the capital and the districts around it, then for the Kaunas region further west. Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons flying NATO's Baltic air policing mission from Šiauliai Air Base destroyed the drone with missile armament, Lithuania's Defense Ministry confirmed, and the army published the first images from the crash site.
The drone was over Lithuanian territory for about half an hour, crisis center head Vilmantas Vitkauskas told LRT radio. He said there is a high probability it carried an explosive charge, though the wreckage does not yet show whether it was a combat drone. Lithuania chose a yellow alert rather than red because red is used when a strike or a fall is unavoidable, he explained, and the drone was destroyed within seconds of the air defense crews reacting, over farmland with no homes nearby.
Military and civilian police are working at the site under the Shield security plan, and the area has been fenced off and guarded. President Gitanas Nausėda thanked the allied personnel for their swift response, saying that with Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine such readiness is vital for the region.
Whose drone it was
Nothing has been established beyond the direction it came from. The army has not commented on the drone's possible origin while the wreckage is still being collected, and the launch point also remains unreleased. Vilnius airport suspended operations during the alert, and flights from Türkiye and Iceland were delayed.
The same night as this incursion, Poland scrambled fighter jets and raised air defense readiness over Russian drone strikes on western Ukraine, and Romania did the same, with neither country recording a violation of its airspace. The day before, the Polish military recovered a drone from the Baltic Sea that its defense minister said preliminary inspection indicated was Russian and military.

articles.title: Is Saudi Arabia recruiting Syrian fighters to fight the Houthis?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Is Saudi Arabia recruiting Syrian fighters to fight the Houthis?
Saudi Arabia has transferred hundreds of Syrian fighters to its southern border for possible deployment against Yemen's Houthis, according to a Lebanese media report, although experts speaking to The New Arab have cast doubt on whether any such deployment has yet taken place.
Lebanon's Al-Akhbar reported this week that hundreds of Syrian fighters had recently arrived in southern Saudi Arabia, including men who took part in the "Deterrence of Aggression" offensive that toppled Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The report comes as Saudi Arabia faces renewed pressure from the Houthis, who have made significant territorial advances in Yemen and launched attacks on Saudi territory.
There has so far been no confirmation from either Riyadh or Damascus that Syrian fighters have been deployed, while several pieces of purported evidence circulating online have been found to be false or misrepresented.
Maysaa Shuja Al-Deen, a senior researcher at the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies, told The New Arab that she had independently heard of discussions within Saudi circles about bringing Syrian fighters into the conflict, but said she was not aware of the proposal having been put into action.
"I heard that the Saudis are thinking about that, but they haven't brought Syrians. They haven't done anything in practice," Shuja Al-Deen said.
Aron Lund, a Middle East analyst with the Swedish Defense Research Agency, told The New Arab that the Al-Akhbar report seems "improbable and overblown", warning that claims of foreign extremist involvement are a "propaganda classic" in regional conflicts.
However, Lund said the possibility could not be entirely dismissed, noting that Syrian mercenaries were previously deployed to Libya and Saudi Arabia had used foreign troops in Yemen.
There was therefore potentially "some little fire behind the smoke", he said, such as Syrian trainers or drone experts, but stressed that this remained speculation in the absence of tangible evidence
Shuja Al-Deen said numerous proposals were circulating as Riyadh considers how to respond to the deteriorating position of forces opposed to the Houthis, including discussions in some Saudi and Western circles about encouraging the UAE to return to a greater role in Yemen.
"There are many talks and discussions and suggestions here and there," she said.
Would Syrian fighters change the war?
Shuja Al-Deen said she had also specifically heard discussion of bringing Salafi or "jihadi" fighters from Syria to Yemen, although she strongly questioned the military logic of the proposal.
"As I told you, there are many talks and discussions here and there, and one of them, as I heard, is that they are going to bring some Salafi or jihadi fighters from Syria," she said, describing the proposal as "the most silly idea for me".
She argued that the anti-Houthi camp's principal problem was not a shortage of fighters or weapons, but the fragmentation of the numerous Yemeni forces opposed to the group.
Yemen's mountainous geography would also present a very different battlefield for Syrian fighters accustomed to fighting in Syria, she said, while the anti-Houthi camp already contains substantial numbers of experienced Yemeni fighters, including Salafi forces.
"I don't think it will help or do anything different, because the issue was not about the military capacity of these groups," Shuja Al-Deen said. "They were big troops. They were capable militarily. They have weapons."
Instead, she said recent battlefield setbacks had exposed longstanding divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.
"The big issue that led to this defeat was the lack of coordination and the absence of unified leadership," she said. "It's important that all of the soldiers of the different military factions receive one order from one leader, which has not happened."
Shuja Al-Deen said disagreements between commanders during recent fighting had left forces without a coherent chain of command.
"The soldiers were lost. There is no one order for everyone," she said. "It was a political issue regarding the division, or the lack of coordination, between the different groups that are fighting the Houthis."
She said that if Syrian fighters were ultimately deployed, she expected it to happen in coordination with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is heavily dependent on Saudi Arabia.
"If it happens, definitely it will happen in coordination with the government," she said, describing the Yemeni government as "a puppet in the hands of the Saudis".
Would Damascus be involved?
The identity of any Syrians potentially being considered for deployment would be significant.
Syria's former opposition factions have undergone a complicated process of incorporation into the country's new armed forces since Assad's fall, meaning the recruitment of former factional fighters would not necessarily indicate an official deployment by Damascus.
There is currently no evidence that the Syrian government has authorised or facilitated the reported plan.
Damascus has, however, publicly backed Saudi Arabia amid the recent escalation. Syria's foreign ministry condemned Houthi attacks on the kingdom earlier this month and expressed solidarity with Riyadh and its right to take measures to protect its security.
The reports emerge as Saudi Arabia struggles to contain a renewed Houthi offensive that has dramatically altered the military picture in Yemen.
The Houthis have captured the strategic port city of Mocha and strengthened their position around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including taking control of Perim and the Hanish Islands.
They have also stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting energy and military infrastructure, while Riyadh has reportedly sought greater US military assistance against the group.
Washington has resisted Saudi requests for direct US attacks on the Houthis, according to Reuters, while continuing to provide intelligence support.
The reported discussions over Syrian fighters come as Riyadh considers how to shore up an anti-Houthi camp that has suffered major battlefield setbacks despite possessing significant numbers of fighters and weapons.
Shuja Al-Deen said bringing in additional foreign fighters would not address what she identified as the central problem - the absence of unified political and military leadership among the Yemeni factions fighting the Houthis.

articles.title: Ex-NATO chief lands Munich Security Conference top job
articles.body:
Ex-NATO chief lands Munich Security Conference top job
Former NATO Secretary-General Jens Stoltenberg will become the co-chair of the Munich Security Conference (MSC) together with the former head of the OSCE, Helga Maria Schmid, the organizers have said.
The conference, which has been held annually in Germany’s third-largest city since 1963, is considered one of the leading Western platforms for security policy and geopolitical debate. It was at the MSC that Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered his famous 2007 speech, criticizing the unipolar world order and NATO’s eastward expansion. Representatives from Moscow were last invited to the gathering in 2022.
The Russian presidential investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, reacted to the appointment of Stoltenberg and Schmid in a post on X on Tuesday, saying that “instead of striving to become a much-needed neutral solution space for global security, the Munich Security Conference reinforces its position as a NATO fiefdom.”
In a statement on the Munich Security Conference website on Monday, Stoltenberg said he was pleased to become one of the co-chairs of the conference and thanked the MSC Foundation Council for “this vote of confidence.” 
“I’m really looking forward to sharing this post with Helga, with whom I’ve already collaborated with excellently in our previous roles at NATO, the EU, and the OSCE,” he said.
The Norwegian politician, who served as NATO secretary-general between 2014 and 2024, was expected to be appointed the sole chairman of the MSC in early 2025. However, Stoltenberg postponed taking up the role repeatedly due to becoming his country’s finance minister around the same time. Becoming a co-chair should allow him to combine his work in the government in Oslo with his duties at the MSC.
Stoltenberg took up the reins at NATO several months after the violent Western-backed coup in Kiev in 2014, which led to the overthrow of democratically-elected Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich. The US-led bloc continued its eastward expansion under his leadership, with Montenegro, North Macedonia, Finland, and Sweden joining it between 2017 and 2024. NATO also continued to increase its military buildup near Russian borders and boosted ties with the new authorities in Kiev, despite repeated protests and warnings by Russia.
After the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, which was largely provoked by Kiev’s aspirations of becoming a NATO member, Stoltenberg consistently advocated for more Western military aid to Vladimir Zelensky’s government, while also calling a Russian victory the “biggest cost and the greatest risk” for the bloc.
In 2024, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called the NATO chief an “irresponsible” person, who failed to grasp the consequences of his actions, after he supported the use of long-range foreign-supplied weapons by Ukraine for strikes deep into Russian territory. Putin reacted to his words by saying that he remembered the times when Stoltenberg “didn’t suffer from dementia.”
Schmid, who was secretary-general of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe between 2020 and 2024, said she was delighted to contribute her “experience in European diplomacy and international negotiations” to the work of the Munich Security Conference.
During Schmid’s tenure, Moscow repeatedly accused the OSCE of being hijacked by its NATO and EU members to advance Western interests at the expense of other members. Earlier this year, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Grushko said the organization was effectively turned into an instrument of “hybrid war and coercion” against sovereign states, who are “subjected to threats, blackmail” for simply pursuing their national interests.
The outgoing MSC chairman, Wolfgang Ischinger, who has been in charge for two decades, will hand over his duties to Stoltenberg and Schmid sometime before February 2027 when the next conference is scheduled to be held.

articles.title: Russia Says Space ‘Must Be Free From Any Weapon’
articles.body:
Russia called Tuesday for weapons to be kept out of space, after the US Space Force confirmed it had deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” for the first time.
“We believe that space must be free of any weapon,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarisation of space,” he added.
Russia’s ally China also on Tuesday slammed Washington’s move, and urged the United States to “stop preparing for war in outer space”.
The United States confirmed on Monday it had weapons deployed for the first time.
“The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons.
“Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain -- employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities,” the statement said, adding that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes.”
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty -- to which the United States, Russia and China are all parties -- bans the deployment of nuclear weapons in space, but is not a blanket ban on military activity.

articles.title: Congress Might Be About to Hand Trump Sweeping Tariff Powers
articles.body:
Congress Might Be About to Hand Trump Sweeping Tariff Powers
The Russia-sanctions bill isn’t what it seems.
The Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, which the House will likely vote on this week, looks like a no-brainer for supporters of Ukraine who have been calling for President Trump to get tougher on Russia.
A large majority of America’s existing sanctions on Russia, which target thousands of government officials and companies, are currently enforced by executive order, meaning that the president can remove them whenever he wants. The Graham bill would turn those sanctions into law: If Trump wanted to end them, he would need Congress’s approval. It also targets a few Russian officials and companies by name, further reducing Trump’s discretion. These provisions help explain why the late Senator Graham, one of Ukraine’s strongest defenders in Congress, originally championed the bill. President Volodymyr Zelensky himself has urged legislators to pass it, as have more than 30 national-security and foreign-policy experts who argue that it’s in Kyiv’s best interest.
But the bill is not what it seems. The legislation would impose no significant new sanctions on Russia, and it would allow Trump to waive any of its measures simply by claiming that doing so is in the national interest. In other words, a law that appears to handcuff Trump would offer him a key to free himself. What’s more, its most important provisions are about not sanctions per se, but tariffs. The bill could provide Trump with the same kind of sweeping authority to impose tariffs that the Supreme Court took away from him in February, allowing him to intensify his trade war with many of America’s allies and partners.
The legislation would give the president authority to impose levies of up to 100 percent on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and the five largest importers of Russian natural gas, which include China, India, France, Japan, Hungary, and Slovakia. It also allows him to impose tariffs on the five countries that are deemed to be the biggest facilitators of Russia’s evasion of oil sanctions—a vague provision largely subject to presidential discretion. (There are a few carve-outs for the natural-gas category, but not for the others.)
Peter Harrell, a trade lawyer who served in the Biden administration, told me that the bill “gives Trump much more flexibility on tariffs than traditional tariff laws. There are no guardrails or restrictions.” The simplest reading of the legislation suggests that Trump can impose tariffs on only the countries that appear in the various top-five lists. But Harrell noted that Trump’s second-term track record suggests that he might try to interpret the law more expansively, perhaps by treating the European Union as a single country and imposing tariffs on the entire bloc all at once. Harrell also warned that the administration might use the law as a pretext to impose tariffs on countries that have little or nothing to do with Russia evading sanctions.
It wouldn’t be the first time that Trump has employed such a pretext. Consider his 25 percent tariff on India, which the Supreme Court has since struck down. The levy was ostensibly meant to punish the country for importing oil from Russia. But reporting suggests that the decision had more to do with Trump’s annoyance that Prime Minister Narendra Modi didn’t give him credit for the cease-fire that India and Pakistan signed last year.
Going beyond the letter of the Graham bill could well result in litigation for the administration. But Trump would still have ample reason to take an aggressive approach. For one thing, the legal process takes a long time—most trade lawyers think that the February ruling came at warp speed, even though it was a year in the making. While the case was moving through the courts, they consistently allowed the Trump administration to continue collecting tariff revenue in the meantime. In all likelihood, Trump would be free to use the tariff tool expansively for most of the rest of his term.
Trump is evidently less worried about Russia evading sanctions than he is about oil prices. At the start of the Iran war, he waived some sanctions on Russian oil in an attempt to keep prices from going up. There is little reason to think that he will act more forcefully against Russian energy now, because oil prices remain high and the midterms are just a month away. Indeed, he has failed to update and enforce sanctions that are already on the books, despite bipartisan support. Moreover, Trump recently sent Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow to dangle the prospect of sanctions relief in exchange for some modest steps toward deescalating the war.
Still, supporters of the bill believe that the benefits outweigh the risks. Eric Ciaramella, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace who served on the National Security Council as an adviser on Ukraine policy in the first Trump administration, told me, “If Trump wanted to hurt Europe, he has lots of ways to do that already. This is just a marginal increase in that risk, and it adds some political pressure on him to get tougher on Russia.” Whether such pressure would get Trump to change, however, is another question.
Perhaps the strongest argument in favor of the bill is simply that the Ukrainians want it. The legislation would no doubt serve as a symbol of Congress’s support. But Ukraine needs material, not symbolic, support—particularly weapons such as air-defense interceptors and greater economic assistance to survive the winter. Trump has the power to provide both, but he has chosen not to. Turning the Graham bill into law isn’t likely to give him a sudden change of heart.
Yesterday, Democrats tried but failed to introduce amendments that would exempt the EU from being treated as a country, tighten the national-security waiver, and scrap the broad allowances for tariffs on countries other than Russia. Without those measures, the bill amounts to little more than a permission slip for Trump to restart his trade war with America’s allies and partners. That’s not a price worth paying just to give Ukraine a symbolic victory.

articles.title: 3rd Army Corps commander confirms Ukrainian offensive near Lyman, promises good news
articles.body:
3rd Army Corps commander confirms Ukrainian offensive near Lyman, promises good news
The 3rd Army Corps has reported mopping up 75 sq km and liberating a further 10 sq km as part of counteroffensive operations in the northern part of Donetsk Oblast.
Source: Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, Commander of the 3rd Army Corps, on social media
Details: The offensive operation is called Vivaldi. The 3rd Corps has so far reported clearing Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova and the outskirts of Korovii Yar of Russian infiltration and liberating Serednie. Biletskyi stressed that Vivaldi has four seasons, called for information silence and promised good news in official updates.
Quote from the 3rd Corps: "We confirm reports of a Ukrainian army offensive in the north of Donetsk Oblast. Maintaining information silence, the units eliminated pockets of enemy infiltration and cleared 75 sq km. A further 10 sq km has been liberated. A devastating blow has been dealt to the combat capability of Russia's 20th and 25th Armies.
Enemy losses at this stage amount to around 1,500 soldiers, more than 12,000 drones and hundreds of armoured vehicles, artillery systems and other vehicles.
Meanwhile, unmanned systems units cut off the enemy's logistics routes. As a result of the Corps' strikes, Russian forces moved their fuel and lubricant supplies outside Ukraine to Voronezh Oblast: a pipeline was shut down and warehouses were destroyed.
This was made possible thanks to the 60th Separate Mechanised Brigade, the 125th Separate Heavy Mechanised Brigade, the battalion tactical group of the 3rd Assault Brigade, the Corps' 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion and 25th Separate Anti-Tank Battalion, as well as attached units – the 66th Separate Mechanised Brigade, the 85th Tactical Group of the 8th Special Operations Forces Regiment, the Artan special unit of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Dozor 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment."
Quote from Biletskyi: "There is currently a lot of information in open sources suggesting that the ultimate goal of our offensive operations is to reach the banks of the Chornyi Zherebets River. But our operation is called Vivaldi. And Vivaldi, as everyone knows, has four seasons. This is only the first of them. So follow our official updates and don't rush to give away spoilers. There will be good news."
Background:
- On 26 August, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast would be reinforced by two restructured military groupings, which are to be led by Denys Prokopenko and Andrii Biletskyi.
- Both officers hold the title of Hero of Ukraine.
