articles.title: German military operates secretive unit to provide arms to Kiev – media
articles.body:
German military operates secretive unit to provide arms to Kiev – media
The German Defense Ministry has a secretive military unit dedicated solely to facilitating cooperation between Berlin and Kiev, including meeting Ukraine’s weapons demands, the Financial Times has reported. Dubbed Sonderstab Ukraine (Special Staff Ukraine), the unit processes arms procurement contracts signed by Kiev under Berlin’s military support program, which amounts to €11.5 billion ($13.27 billion) this year alone.
Described by one of the FT’s sources as an “incredibly un-German” unit, Special Staff Ukraine prides itself on signing off on Kiev’s demands in less than two weeks while bypassing the standard procurement rules that apply to Germany’s own armed forces, the Bundeswehr. The arrangement is possible because Ukraine, rather than Berlin, signs the contracts, according to the FT.
“Kiev provided the shopping list. Berlin paid the bill,” the outlet said, describing the unit’s operations. The FT said it enjoys strong political backing from German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius.
Created soon after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, the unit was initially tasked with monitoring the fighting and briefing Berlin’s political leadership on developments. Several months later, it pivoted heavily toward facilitating military support for Kiev.
The unit was formed and initially led by Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, who now heads the nation’s Land Forces. Known for his hardline stance on Russia, Freuding claimed in March that a full-fledged conflict between Russia and NATO could occur as early as 2029 and said Ukrainian military instructors would help the German military train for the allegedly looming confrontation.
The unit’s current commander, Brigadier General Joachim Kaschke, told the FT that it was entirely up to Kiev how to spend the German money. “We are not there to advise them – there is no ‘mentoring’,” he stated, adding that Berlin simply connects the relevant Ukrainian officials with German arms manufacturers.
At some point, cooperation between Berlin and Kiev expanded beyond simple arms exports, with Ukrainian companies gaining access to the NATO market through joint ventures with German partners, alarming German arms manufacturers. “The situation with Ukraine has changed, and it’s trying to become an exporter as well as an importer,” a defense contractor executive told the FT. “It’s becoming more political.”
Berlin has also complained that Kiev is not spending enough of its Western-provided procurement funds on German weapons. Last week, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul warned that Germany would struggle to justify its continued support for Ukraine to its people if it did not bring any benefits.
“We stand by you, we support you. But I also have to explain this to German taxpayers, and the very least you can do is to involve the German defense industry in all procurement measures,” Wadephul told Bild.
Germany emerged as Kiev’s single biggest military donor after the US drastically scaled back its assistance under President Donald Trump. Berlin has provided or earmarked a total of €57.6 billion in military aid for Ukraine, according to German government data.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has prioritized a military buildup, including assistance to Kiev, despite acknowledging that Germany’s economy is in a “structural crisis.” His government amended the constitutional debt brake to fund the buildup and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion to defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Ukraine. The spending comes despite warnings from the German central bank that the country is on course to record its largest budget deficit since reunification by 2028.

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges partners not to ease Russia sanctions, adopt Graham bill on new restrictions
articles.body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on international partners not to lift sanctions against Russia and to introduce new, stronger restrictions, particularly targeting Russian ballistic missile production and the financial sector, as well as to adopt the sanctions bill introduced by late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham.
"And new sanctions are needed. And, to be honest, stronger ones. Ones that Russia cannot adapt to," he said in a video address on Monday.
Zelenskyy emphasized that sanctions against Russia matter and that now is "definitely not the time" to lift them or help Russian oligarchs evade restrictions.
He noted that Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov, Mikhail Fridman, and other representatives of Russian business have still not taken steps against the war.
According to the President, sanctions are specifically needed against all Russian ballistic weapons manufacturing and restrictions on the Russian financial sector.
"Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill is still a bill. Unfortunately, not a law. It is important that it becomes law," Zelenskyy stated.
He also urged Europe not to forget about the war and not to make concessions to Russia.
"I thank everyone who supports this approach. Who knows that strength, strength works," the President added.

articles.title: Volker: Ukraine knows how to shoot down drones cheaply, NATO must adopt this experience
articles.body:
Former U.S. Special Representative for Ukraine (2017–19) and Kyiv Security Forum (KSF) Security Council member Kurt Volker has expressed the conviction that NATO should cooperate with Ukraine to create an integrated air picture in order to counter the infiltration of drones and missiles.
Volker noted during a special meeting of the KSF Security Council in Kyiv that he would like NATO to start cooperating with Ukraine on establishing an integrated air picture and setting up a no-fly zone around NATO airspace together with Ukraine to eliminate the problem of drones, missiles, and other objects penetrating the Alliance's territory, adding that this is one of the ways to support Ukraine.
He specified that this involves closing the airspace around the Alliance's territory at a certain distance, emphasizing that they must support Ukraine's efforts to close the airspace around NATO territory, perhaps at a distance of 150 kilometers.
Separately, the ambassador stressed that NATO countries should adopt Ukrainian experience in countering air threats, adding that they must learn from Ukrainians how to shoot down missiles and drones in a cost-effective manner, something NATO countries have not yet undertaken to do.
He also named three key elements of Ukraine's strategy that he believes the West must strengthen: striking Russian finances, pressuring the war economy, and exhausting the Russian military. Volker emphasized that it is necessary to do everything possible to strike the Kremlin's finances, noting that Russia primarily receives money from oil and gas sales and must be deprived of this source of revenue, and that Russians are feeling the consequences of the war, seeing them in the form of fires, smoke, and fuel lines, with this overall impact on the Russian economy creating pressure on Putin domestically.
Volker stressed that the West must strengthen these areas, in particular through secondary sanctions, stating that they must target the Kremlin's finances and adopt Senator Lindsey Graham's bill, with special attention paid to secondary sanctions against financial institutions that process payments in favor of Russia.
The special meeting of the KSF Security Council was dedicated to the challenges awaiting Ukraine this winter. Its participants, in addition to Volker, included KSF Chairman and former Prime Minister (2014–16) Arseniy Yatsenyuk and former U.S. Central Command Commander (2008–10) and former CIA Director (2011–12) David Petraeus.

The Middle East stands on the precipice of a new nuclear age, with Saudi Arabia set to acquire American uranium enrichment technology and Turkey eager to follow suit, as Iran weighs withdrawal from the treaty that bars it from making atomic bombs.

articles.title: UK to send advisors to Saudi as experts warn over Yemen role
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK to send military advisors to Saudi Arabia as experts warn over Yemen war role
The UK has sent military advisors to Saudi Arabia as the kingdom confronts a renewed Houthi offensive in Yemen, with experts telling The New Arab that renewed British support risks deepening London's role in a conflict that has caused a devastating humanitarian crisis.
Bloomberg reported that the UK had sent military advisors to assist Saudi Arabia and was considering providing military aid to the kingdom, as Riyadh faces renewed pressure from the Houthis.
Sam Perlo-Freeman, research coordinator at the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), told The New Arab that the renewed British support was deeply concerning given London's previous role in arming and supporting the Saudi-led campaign in Yemen.
"The UK was deeply involved in arming and supporting Saudi in this absolutely horrific conflict, and it is absolutely appalling that we are seeing this pattern repeating itself," Perlo-Freeman said.
He said the renewed assistance was unsurprising given the scale of military trade between Britain and Saudi Arabia.
"Just recently, the government published its latest arms export licensing statistics for quarter one of 2026, which showed that there was over £416 million worth of export licenses to Saudi Arabia in the ML four category, which covers bombs, missiles, etc," he said.
"It's unfortunately not surprising that the UK is wanting to offer more support yet to its closest Middle East ally, but it's a terrible idea," he added.
Saudi Arabia, one of Britain's closest military partners, has been involved in Yemen's civil war since 2015, when it launched airstrikes against the Houthis at the request of Abed Rabbo Mansour Hadi, who was Yemen's president at the start of the war.
The kingdom has continued its military involvement in the conflict on and off over the past 11 years. Saudi military action has included attacks on civilian targets, such as strikes on a ceramics factory in 2015 and a community college in 2016. CAAT has reported that weapons originating in the UK were used in both strikes.
The renewed British involvement comes as Saudi Arabia faces a deteriorating position in Yemen after the Houthis made significant territorial gains and stepped up attacks on Saudi territory.
Saudi Arabia's most recent military involvement in Yemen began earlier this month after the Houthis captured the port of Mocha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping route for Saudi oil.
The Bab al-Mandab Strait has similar strategic significance to the Strait of Hormuz, which was effectively closed by Iran in March in retaliation for US-Israel strikes on the country. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for Gulf oil, caused a global surge in oil prices.
Abdul Shaif, chairman of the UK-based Friends of South Yemen advocacy group, warned that further fighting around the Bab al-Mandab could have serious consequences for Yemen's already dire humanitarian situation.
"If there is renewed fighting in that area of the world, that will also affect transport routes, which could affect the movement of food, fuel, and aid into Yemen, both in the north and in the south," Shaif told The New Arab.
"I think that dimension needs to be taken very, very seriously because if you disturb the supply lines of food that will only make matters much, much worse," he added.
The latest UN figures show about 94,000 people displaced in Yemen since the fighting intensified this month, with the number still rising.
The UK Foreign Office has not yet responded to The New Arab's request for comment.

articles.title: Ukrainian RAM-2X drone strikes US$100m Russian radar – video
articles.body:
Ukrainian RAM-2X drone strikes US$100m Russian radar – video
The 429th Achilles Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade has posted a video showing how, together with the 43rd Separate Artillery Brigade, it struck a Russian Nebo-M radar system near the Millerovo military airfield.
Source: 429th Achilles Brigade on YouTube
Details: The brigade did not disclose the date of the strike.
"The strike was carried out by a RAM-2X loitering munition at a distance of about 175 km from the line of contact. The estimated average cost of a Nebo-M radar system is US$100 million," the military said.
The brigade noted that the Russians use Millerovo airfield to launch strike and decoy drones, including Shaheds, against Ukraine's east, centre and north.
The Nebo-M is a Russian mobile radar system designed to detect aerodynamic and ballistic targets at medium and high altitudes. According to the 429th Brigade, it can detect aircraft at a range of up to 500-600 km, ballistic targets at up to 1,500 km, and low-observable aerial assets at a range of 200-400 km.
The system can detect small targets, including drones and cruise missiles, at distances ranging from tens to hundreds of kilometres, usually within 50-150 km.
RAM-2X by Ukrspecsystems was designed to strike high-value targets at ranges of up to 180 km. The drone can remain airborne for more than two hours and has a high degree of automation. It can carry a 2.7 kg or 3.5 kg explosively formed penetrator warhead.
Background: Earlier, it was reported that pilots from the 429th Achilles Brigade had struck a Russian Nebo-U radar system at the Millerovo airfield in Russia's Rostov Oblast.

articles.title: 225 combat clashes at frontline in past day, most active in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka – General Staff
articles.body:
Since the beginning of the day, Russian troops have attacked the positions of the Ukrainian Defense Forces 225 times, with the enemy being most active in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has reported.
"In total, 225 combat clashes have occurred since the beginning of this day. The aggressor launched 55 airstrikes using 190 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,183 kamikaze drones for strikes, and carried out 1,724 shellings of our troops' positions and settlements," the statement reads.
In North Slobozhanske and Kursk directions, two enemy assault operations have been recorded since the beginning of the day. The enemy launched one airstrike using a single guided aerial bomb and carried out 50 shellings of Ukrainian troops' positions and settlements.
In South Slobozhanske direction, the enemy attacked Ukrainian units three times toward the settlements of Kozacha Lopan, Lyman, and Obukhivka.
In Kupiansk direction, the enemy attempted to improve its positions by conducting eight assault operations toward Radkivka, Tyshenkivka, Monachynivka, and Kindrashivka. Five of these attacks are still ongoing.
Six attempts by the invaders to advance were repled in the Lyman direction near the settlements of Novoيهorivka, Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman, and Yampil.
In Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces halted seven attempts by the invaders to advance in the area of the settlements of Ozerne, Kryva Luka, and Mykolaivka. Two battles are ongoing.
In Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 27 enemy assaults near the settlement of Kostiantynivka and toward Novoselivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, Rusyn Yar, Toretske, Vilsne, and Stepove. Two attacks are ongoing.
The enemy launched 22 attacks in the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the settlements of Hannivka, Bilytske, Dobropillia, Svitle, Matiasheve, Serhiivka, Udachne, Molodetske, and Novopidhorodne. One assault operation is still continuing.
"According to preliminary estimates, 62 occupiers were eliminated and 15 wounded here today; six motor vehicles, a special asset, two UAV control posts, a fuel and lubricants depot, and 36 personnel shelters were destroyed. Five motor vehicles, nine UAV control posts, and 123 personnel shelters were damaged. 298 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed," the text states.
In Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled five enemy attacks near the settlements of Rizdvianka, Dobropillia, and Charivne. One of these assaults is still ongoing.
In Orikhiv direction, the enemy attempted to advance toward Shcherbaky and Stepnohirsk.

articles.title: Poland can’t arrest its way out of Russia’s spy pipeline—107 espionage cases in 20 months, and the tempo is holding
articles.body:
Sabotage preparation, remote recruitment, and data collection on military sites account for a significant share of Poland's espionage docket, and public arrests have not dented the pace, RBC-Ukraine reported on 15 September. The published figures cover only the highest-complexity investigations, so with district prosecutors' cases counted in, the real scale of Russian activity is larger still.
Russia's covert campaign inside the EU has escalated from online disinformation into physical attacks since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine—arson at defense plants, assassination plots, and bomb-rigged drones found at European airports.
Recorded sabotage incidents across Europe tripled between 2023 and 2024 alone. Poland, as NATO's primary overland corridor for Western military aid to Ukraine, sits at the center of that pressure—its railway routes near the Rzeszów logistics hub have drawn particular attention.
What the prosecutors count as espionage
Poland's National Prosecutor's Office opened 67 criminal cases under Article 130 of the Criminal Code—espionage and activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service—during 2025, spokesperson Przemysław Nowak told RBC-Ukraine. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, prosecutors added at least 40 more.
At that pace, 2026 could yield roughly 60 new cases, RBC-Ukraine noted, concluding that the tempo of recruitment and sabotage preparation is not slowing but staying steadily high despite public detentions and strengthened counterintelligence.
Courier bombs and expendable operatives
Earlier, Polish law enforcement exposed two Russian citizens prosecutors say worked for Russian special services. One of them planned to send an explosive device through a delivery service—part of a wider Russian sabotage campaign that recruits low-cost, expendable operatives for arson and disruption across the EU.

articles.title: Drone-hit Saudi oil pipeline to remain non-operational for weeks – AP
articles.body:
Drone-hit Saudi oil pipeline to remain non-operational for weeks – AP
A key Saudi Arabian oil pipeline hit in a drone strike by Iraqi militias will take up to five weeks to repair, AP has reported, citing informed officials.
The East-West Pipeline, which runs 1,200 km across the country towards the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, will remain mostly out of service during the three- to five-week repair period, the agency said in an article on Tuesday.
One official suggested that parts of the infrastructure could function while segments of the pipeline and a major pumping station are being fixed, but couldn’t say how much oil might get through, according to AP.
Oil prices spiked by more than 3% on Monday, with benchmark Brent crude reaching $109 per barrel, following the decision by the Saudi authorities to shut down the pipeline after it was struck by drones in the Riyadh and Medina areas on Thursday.
The Gulf kingdom blamed Iranian-backed militias in Iraq for the attack, with the government in Baghdad confirming that the UAVs came from Iraqi territory and condemning the aggression.
According to some reports, Iraqi fighters targeted the pipeline in solidarity with Yemen’s Houthis, officially known as the Ansarallah movement, who made major gains along Yemeni Red Sea coast last week, pushing back Saudi-supported forces and seizing the ports of Mocha and Dhubab as well as key islands at the entrance to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping chokepoint.
Saudi Arabia, which is the world’s largest supplier of oil, shifted its exports from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea as the Strait of Hormuz remains shut due to the conflict between the US and Iran.
The Houthis further tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Monday, capturing the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish without a fight, AP reported, citing officials from the group and Saudi-backed forces.
The Yemeni group said on the same day that it had fired dozens of missiles and drones at the King Khalid Air Base in the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
The attack “was accurate and caused heavy damage” to aircraft hangars, radars, landing strips, and ammunition depots at the facility, Houthi military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said.
The strike was “a response to the escalation of tension by the Saudi regime and the implementation of more than 300 airstrikes in the past five days,” Saree stressed.
Saudi military spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said 13 civilians were wounded during the Houthi raid on Khamis Mushait, but didn’t confirm the attack on the airbase.
Riyadh has asked Britain for military support in stemming the Houthi advance in Yemen and repelling strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure, Bloomberg reported on Monday.
Last week, US President Donald Trump reportedly declined several requests by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to order airstrikes against the Houthis.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has so far only agreed to send military advisers to Saudi Arabia, the agency said. Burnham is hesitant to provide further assistance due to concerns of it being viewed as him backing Trump’s war on Iran, which is deeply unpopular in Britain, Bloomberg said.

articles.title: Pentagon unsure about ‘future posture’ in Middle East
articles.body:
Pentagon unsure about ‘future posture’ in Middle East
The Pentagon has yet to determine the future posture of US forces in the Middle East, including how regional bases damaged in the conflict with Iran will be rebuilt, according to a new government report examining Operation Epic Fury.
The US military operation against Iran lasted from February 28 through June 30, although the confrontation remains unresolved, with Washington relying on a naval blockade and sanctions to pressure Tehran. Iran responded to the US-Israeli attack by striking military and infrastructure targets across the region and restricting traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
The report, prepared by three inspector general offices and released on Monday, highlighted difficulties in determining the full cost of Operation Epic Fury. The Pentagon estimated the campaign had cost $33.4 billion as of June 29, excluding the reconstruction of damaged military infrastructure.
During congressional appropriations hearings in May, the department did not include military reconstruction costs because it “has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs Allies and partners will contribute,” the report said.
Iranian attacks forced US Central Command (CENTCOM) to move operations away from bases close to Iran, significantly disrupting established supply lines. The US Navy base in Bahrain, a major regional logistics hub, could no longer properly support maritime operations, forcing the military to rely on alternative facilities farther away.
The change “posed significant challenges before and during” the operation, CENTCOM told Pentagon Inspector General Platte Moring, who led the joint oversight effort.
“An issue with shifting logistics support and infrastructure to Diego Garcia has been distance, with extended sea transit requiring 14- to 18-day logistics cycles,” the report said.
The increased reliance on military facilities on the Chagos Islands, operated jointly by the US and British militaries, became a source of friction between US President Donald Trump and then-British Prime Minister Keir Starmer during the first phase of the Iran war.
US media have linked problems experienced by the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier strike group during its deployment to the roughly 2,200-mile (3,500-kilometer) supply route between Diego Garcia and the Middle East.
The report to Congress also detailed bottlenecks exposed by Pentagon efforts to replenish munitions consumed during the operation.
The most persistent problems “remain in the production of solid rocket motors, the availability of high-grade explosives and propellants, and the recruitment of skilled manufacturing labor,” the report said, describing the resulting inventory shortfalls as “strategic.”
The 40-page document was prepared by the inspector general offices overseeing the Department of War, the State Department, and the shuttered US Agency for International Development.

articles.title: Ukrainian military strikes Ozon warehouse and oil refinery in Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian military strikes Ozon warehouse and oil refinery in Russia
Ukrainian drones and missiles struck Taganrog overnight on September 15, damaging a warehouse belonging to the marketplace Ozon along with several residential buildings, stores, and administrative buildings, Rostov Governor Yuri Slyusar said. No one was injured, according to the governor.
Ozon said a logistics partner’s delivery hub in Taganrog was evacuated over a missile threat. The company said goods from sellers “were never accepted” at the hub, adding that “it performs other operations.”
The Ukrainian monitoring project Exilenova+ said one of the strike’s targets was the G.V. Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex, which repairs and upgrades military aircraft.
Ukrainian drones also struck Russia’s Samara region, damaging one industrial facility, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said without elaborating. The independent Telegram channel Astra and Ukrainian monitoring channels reported that the target was Rosneft’s Syzran oil refinery.
On September 14, US President Donald Trump said that Ukraine had agreed not to strike Russian energy infrastructure — and that Russia had allegedly agreed to do the same. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Ukraine’s readiness for such a deal but voiced doubt that Russia would follow through. Financial Times sources said that Trump had jumped the gun in announcing the energy truce.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Russian Tu-95 Strategic Bomber Repair Hub Reportedly Targeted in Taganrog Missile Strike
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Tu-95 Strategic Bomber Repair Hub Reportedly Targeted in Taganrog Missile Strike
A missile attack struck the Russian city of Taganrog overnight on September 15, with preliminary reports indicating that the Beriev aviation complex, a key facility involved in repairing and modernizing Russia’s Tu-95 strategic bombers, may have been among the targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rostov region governor Yuri Slyusar confirmed what he described as a large-scale missile attack on the city. According to his statement, the strike damaged agricultural warehouses, an Ozon logistics warehouse, a commercial building, a grocery store, a gas pipeline, several residential buildings, and an educational facility. Several fires were also reported.
According to Supernova+ and other monitoring channels on September 15, explosions and smoke were reported near the Beriev Taganrog Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex. The channels also reported that Russian military aircraft were undergoing repairs at the facility at the time of the attack.
The exact extent of any damage to the aviation complex has not yet been independently confirmed.
The Beriev plant is one of Russia’s major military aviation maintenance facilities and has been involved in repairing and modernizing Tu-95MS strategic bombers, aircraft used by Russia to launch long-range cruise missiles against Ukraine.
Defense Express previously reported that documents leaked in 2025 revealed a contract worth approximately $200 million for the repair of three Tu-95MS bombers at the Taganrog facility. The work was valued at roughly $66 million per aircraft.
According to Defense Express, the nature of the work indicated that the aircraft could have been undergoing modernization toward the Tu-95MSM configuration, which includes upgrades allowing the bombers to carry additional Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles.
The Beriev complex also repairs and modernizes other Russian military aircraft and operates its own Taganrog-Yuzhny airfield. The city is also home to the Taganrog-Central military airfield and the 325th Aircraft Repair Plant, making it an important aviation maintenance hub for the Russian military.
The Beriev facility has been targeted previously. In November 2025, Ukrainian forces struck military-industrial facilities in Taganrog. Ukraine’s General Staff later reported that an experimental A-60 aircraft may have been destroyed during the attack.
The September 15 strike followed another attack on Taganrog several days earlier, when fires were reported near aviation and industrial facilities in the city.
Earlier, satellite imagery confirmed significant damage to Russia’s Volgogradpromproekt chemical plant after a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile strike. The facility supplies materials used in Russian weapons production, including components linked to Iskander-M, Kinzhal, Kalibr, Grad, Smerch, and Tornado-S systems.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force stacks its next nuclear missile for first time
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman vertically assembled a fully integrated inert Sentinel ICBM at Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 14, 2026.
- The milestone and a completed Critical Design Review confirm the missile's design maturity ahead of a planned 2027 flight test.
The U.S. Air Force and Northrop Grumman have fully assembled an inert version of the Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the company announced Sept. 14, 2026. The vertical assembly is a step toward flight testing the missile in 2027.
Engineers stacked all of the missile’s stages, propulsion elements, and its protective shroud into a single configuration on the test pad, according to Northrop Grumman. The operation was designed to prove that the process for safely assembling a complete Sentinel missile actually works in practice, not just on paper.
Getting the inert missile onto the pad took a four-month effort. Northrop Grumman moved missile components from facilities around the country to Vandenberg, then used specialized transport equipment and mobile cranes to stack the sections and later take them apart again. The company said the exercise, including verification of how each section’s interfaces connect, showed the team is ready to move toward an actual flight test.
Alongside the assembly, Northrop Grumman and the U.S. Air Force’s 719th Test Squadron completed the program’s first flight test Critical Design Review. The review confirmed that Sentinel’s design and hardware testing meet the Air Force’s requirements for performance, safety, and schedule ahead of the planned 2027 flight test.
“This vertical assembly demonstrates the momentum toward test launching Sentinel in 2027 and having missiles on alert by the early 2030s, ensuring the United States’ ground-based nuclear capabilities remain strong and reliable for decades to come,” said Amanda Davis, vice president and general manager of strategic deterrent systems at Northrop Grumman.
Sentinel, formally designated the LGM-35A, is meant to replace the Minuteman III missiles that have formed the ground-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad since the early 1970s. The Air Force’s plan calls for fielding 659 missiles and modernizing 450 launch silos and associated facilities, a scope that goes well beyond simply swapping out the missile itself.
Northrop Grumman won the original engineering and manufacturing contract in 2020, valued at $13.3 billion. By January 2024, cost growth on the program had triggered a critical breach under the Nunn-McCurdy Act, the law that requires the Pentagon to report major acquisition cost overruns to Congress.
A Pentagon review that July found the overrun had grown to 81 percent above the original baseline, pushing the total program cost estimate to roughly $140.9 billion. Defense officials certified the program to continue but ordered it restructured and pushed the expected fielding timeline back by at least three years.
Sept. 14’s assembly and design review mark the program’s most concrete hardware milestone since that restructuring. Northrop Grumman has not said how many additional assembly cycles or test events are planned between now and the 2027 flight test, and the Air Force has not released an updated cost or schedule baseline beyond the 2024 figures.

articles.title: U.S. Air Force secretary confirms U.S. has weapons in orbit
articles.body:
- Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said the United States has space-control weapons on orbit capable of defending U.S. forces against hostile adversaries.
- Meink did not specify the weapons' type, quantity, or capabilities, and a space security expert called the disclosure unprecedented for a U.S. official.
U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink confirmed Monday that the United States has weapons in orbit designed to disable or destroy adversary satellites, a rare public admission from a senior Pentagon official about a capability the government has typically declined to discuss, Defense One reported.
Meink made the statement during a Monday morning speech at the Air, Space & Cyber conference. He did not specify what type of weapons the U.S. has stationed in orbit or how many exist.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said.
“This is why the United States now has, on orbit, space-control weapons, capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversaries,” he said.
The comment marks a departure from how top U.S. Space Force and Air Force officials have generally discussed the subject. Gen. John Raymond, the U.S. Space Force’s first chief of space operations, said in 2022 that “our primary purpose is to deter war.” Senior officials have more often cited national security concerns as a reason to avoid confirming specific orbital weapons capabilities.
Victoria Samson, chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, told Defense One she could not recall a prior instance of a U.S. government official making a comparable statement.
“Well, that’s huge, because I don’t think any US government official has ever said that before,” Samson said.
She said the admission could prompt China and Russia, the U.S. military’s principal competitors in space, to be more open about their own orbital weapons programs.
“The US also now has to accept the Chinese and Russians doing/saying the same. I don’t think that this is going to be in the interest of US national security,” Samson said.
Meink’s silence on specifics left outside experts guessing at what the capability might be. Kinetic weapons, such as missiles designed to physically strike a satellite, generate orbital debris that can threaten other spacecraft, including those belonging to the country that fired the weapon. Senior military officials have repeatedly cautioned against their use for that reason.
Maj. Gen. Chris Povak, deputy director of the National Reconnaissance Office, said earlier this year that “our commitment to responsible space operations is fundamental to our mission assurance and our role as stewards of the space environment.”
Samson pointed to that pattern of statements from officials as a reason to rule out a kinetic weapon.
“I’m going to guess what he’s talking about is not a kinetic space-control weapon due to multiple comments government officials have said about avoiding debris causing counter space,” she said. “So I’m going to go with my first guess: space-based jammers, electronic warfare.”
Meink used the same speech to disclose progress on two other space programs, according to Defense One. He said prototype satellites for the space-based Airborne Moving Target Indicator constellation, which is designed to track moving targets from orbit, will launch this month.
He also said space-based interceptors, the technology at the center of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense program, are now “flight ready.”
The interceptor effort has faced funding uncertainty. Space Force Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome’s direct-reporting program manager, warned last month that the project would be in dire straits if Congress does not commit additional money. Guetlein said at the time that initial development work on the interceptors was underway and that the Space Force had completed two “phenomenally successful” tests.
“All of the providers that are part of the competition are progressing exceptionally well,” Guetlein told reporters at the Space and Missile Defense Symposium.
Meink framed the disclosures around competition from rival powers developing their own counter-space capabilities.
“As everybody knows, there have been many who are developing capabilities to take those away from us, to threaten those things,” Meink said. “So, it is critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space, and so that we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
The Air Force secretary did not disclose a timeline for revealing further details about the on-orbit weapons, and the Department of War has not issued a follow-up statement expanding on his remarks.

articles.title: Lawmakers push for Iran's withdrawal from NPT
articles.body:
The statement, said the NPT is based on a reciprocal balance of "commitment to non-proliferation" and "guaranteeing members' rights and security," but recent years and especially recent developments have proven that international structures based on the treaty have become completely ineffective, structurally discriminatory and incapable of securing Iran's minimum legal rights.
The lawmakers listed four reasons for the necessity and urgency of Iran's withdrawal from the NPT and the defining new scientific, technical and legal cooperation with aligned countries.
First, they said the treaty has been ineffective in securing the safety of nuclear facilities. Peaceful facilities under supervision should enjoy the highest level of international protection and immunity from any threat or military attack, but responsible bodies have taken no deterrent action against open threats and attacks on Iran's nuclear centres, effectively endorsing the aggression through silence and passivity.
Second, they cited enemy attacks on infrastructure and the assassination of scientists, including direct attacks, organised sabotage, two recent imposed wars, the assassination of nuclear scientists and repeated threats by U.S. and Israeli officials to launch nuclear strikes against Iran. These, they said, are undeniable evidence that accepting maximum supervision has brought Iran no security and has become a tool for identifying and targeting the country's power components.
Third, they said Iran has been completely deprived of the NPT's legal benefits. Despite fully implementing its obligations and accepting unprecedented supervision, Iran has always been denied its rights under Article 4 of the treaty, especially non-discriminatory access to peaceful technology and international cooperation, and has instead faced the harshest unjust and illegal sanctions.
Fourth, they said the IAEA's inspections have become a cover for industrial and security espionage and continuous political pressure rather than a tool for verification, the latest example being the unjustified referral of Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council.
The statement cited Article 10 of the NPT, which gives any member the right to withdraw from the treaty if it decides that extraordinary events related to the subject matter of the treaty have jeopardised its supreme interests, with three months' notice to all members and the UN Security Council.
The lawmakers said that with continued existential threats, open aggression against Iran's territory and facilities, and the absolute ineffectiveness of international guarantees, Iran's supreme interests and national security are in serious jeopardy and an extraordinary situation.
They called on the parliament's presiding board to activate the legal process for Iran's full withdrawal from the NPT and defining new international cooperation with Iran's friends as quickly as possible, in accordance with parliament's internal regulations.
MNA

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone campaign is changing where Putin goes – now his flagship forum is being moved out of Sochi
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has moved his flagship foreign policy conference from Sochi to Moscow Oblast amid growing concerns over Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes, the Financial Times reported on 15 September.
The decision is likely an indirect acknowledgment of the impact of Ukraine’s ongoing deep-strike drone campaign. Russian officials may not publicly admit that Ukrainian drones pose a serious threat, but their actions suggest otherwise: Putin has increasingly avoided areas within range of Ukrainian drones, and now a major Kremlin event is being moved out of Sochi because of security concerns.
The annual Valdai Discussion Club meeting was originally planned for Sochi, but the venue was changed after Putin’s security service insisted on the move, according to four people familiar with the decision cited by the FT. Some 120 guests had already received invitations to the Black Sea resort before being informed of the change in August.
Putin has not visited Sochi since the Valdai conference there in early October 2025. Since then, Ukraine has significantly stepped up its long-range drone campaign against Russia. The change is stark compared with 2021, when Putin visited the Black Sea resort 24 times, according to the FT.
Ukraine is targeting the defenses behind Russia’s rear
Ukraine has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to strike targets in Russia’s rear. Its drones have reached energy and logistics infrastructure thousands of kilometers from Ukraine, while Sochi and other areas of Russia’s Black Sea coast have come under repeated attack.
The latest strike came on 13–14 September, when Ukraine’s Defense Forces hit the 92N6 multifunction radar of a Russian S-400 air defense system in Sochi, according to Ukraine’s General Staff. The radar tracks aerial targets and guides the S-400’s missiles, making it a critical component of the system defending the area.
The strike followed a 4 September Ukrainian attack on Sochi that hit two fuel depots and an air defense position near the Abkhazia border. Satellite imagery later showed nine destroyed fuel storage tanks and damage at the air defense position.
Putin’s movements show the threat is changing
The relocation also fits a broader pattern in Putin’s movements. The Russian president has spent much of his time in Moscow, St Petersburg and his residence near Lake Valdai in Novgorod Oblast, while making more trips east of the Urals – areas farther from Ukraine’s long-range drone reach.
The Valdai forum will still take place from 28 September to 1 October, but now in Moscow Oblast rather than Sochi. Putin traditionally attends the final day and holds a lengthy question-and-answer session.
The Kremlin does not need to say Ukrainian drones are a serious threat. Moving Putin’s major foreign-policy forum away from Sochi says it for them.

articles.title: The Baltic states fear a Russian invasion. They faced the same threat a century ago and failed to stop it. Historian Alexey Uvarov explains why the region could not defend itself against Stalin.
articles.body:
The Baltic states fear a Russian invasion. They faced the same threat a century ago and failed to stop it. Historian Alexey Uvarov explains why the region could not defend itself against Stalin.
As Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine enters its fifth year, experts and Western intelligence sources are increasingly warning that Russia also poses a growing threat to countries in the Baltic region. So far, the confrontation has produced only isolated incidents, such as drone incursions into these countries’ territory — but tensions are rising. Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Poland, and Finland increasingly need to consider how they would collectively defend themselves against a full-scale invasion from the east. The problem is not new to the region: 100 years ago, the Baltic countries also tried to join forces to protect themselves from militarily stronger neighbors. They failed to create an effective defense alliance. In this article for Meduza, historian and memory-politics expert Alexey Uvarov examines lessons from the Baltic region’s failed efforts to build an effective defense alliance.
The security order around the Baltic Sea has changed significantly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Finland and Sweden have joined NATO, while the Baltic states and Poland have accelerated their rearmament and efforts to strengthen the alliance’s eastern flank. Disputes within NATO over burden-sharing have also intensified: President Donald Trump’s administration is demanding that Europe rely more on its own resources and spend more on defense, while Europeans are increasingly debating whether they can still count on the same level of American involvement in the alliance.
This leaves the countries of the Baltic region facing an old question: To what extent can they ensure their own security, both independently and through regional cooperation, if outside guarantees prove less reliable than before?
One hundred years ago, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland tried to solve a similar problem. After World War I, they formed regional alliances, signed agreements, and drew up joint military plans. By 1939, however, these efforts had failed to produce a functioning system of collective defense. That failure illustrates the limits of a regional alliance without a powerful outside guarantor.
How did the countries of the Baltic region first try to form an alliance?
After World War I, the idea of such an alliance seemed entirely natural. A chain of independent states stretching from Finland to Poland had emerged from the former Russian Empire. Most had just fought the Bolsheviks, and their borders had yet to be firmly settled. Nor was there any certainty that Russia would remain weak for long. Latvia and its first foreign minister, Zigfrīds Meierovics, were especially active in promoting the idea of a “Greater Baltic Union.” Between 1919 and 1925, representatives from countries across the region held 15 conferences on cooperation.
The most ambitious attempt came in the summer of 1920 at a conference in the Latvian resort town of Bulduri. Representatives from Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland attended. They discussed issues ranging from economic and diplomatic cooperation to the creation of a political union. On August 30, the participants even adopted a draft agreement establishing such an alliance. But the conflict that would dog every subsequent effort to unite the region was already apparent: the prospective allies could not agree among themselves. Lithuania refused to sign the agreement, and Poland and Finland later failed to ratify it.
The main obstacle was the Polish-Lithuanian conflict over Vilnius. In the fall of 1920, Polish forces commanded by General Lucjan Żeligowski seized the city, which Lithuania regarded as its capital. After that, it became nearly impossible to imagine Warsaw and Kaunas — Lithuania’s temporary capital from 1920 to 1940 — in the same defense bloc. Yet Poland remained an important partner for Estonia and Latvia in containing Soviet Russia. This created a paradox. On the one hand, the countries agreed that each was vulnerable to outside threats on its own. On the other, they could not agree on who posed the greatest threat or which countries they were prepared to defend together.
Still, they did not immediately abandon the idea of a broad alliance. In March 1922, the foreign ministers of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Poland met in Warsaw and signed a new agreement. It prohibited the parties from entering into treaties directed against one another and called for coordinated action in the event of an external threat. But it fell short of a full military alliance: if one country came under unprovoked attack, the others were required to adopt a “benevolent” attitude toward it and agree on further measures. The treaty did not require them to go to war.
But even this agreement never took effect. It sparked fierce debate in Finland: most parties considered the new foreign policy commitments too risky, and Parliament refused to ratify it. Helsinki subsequently became much more cautious about proposed alliances with the Baltic states and Poland. In the years that followed, it increasingly turned toward neutrality and cooperation with the Scandinavian countries. Finnish politicians feared that joining a Baltic bloc might not make their country safer and could instead draw it into a conflict over its allies’ interests. The Warsaw Agreement never entered into force.
Rather than forming a single broad alliance, countries in the region began pursuing smaller alliances. Estonia and Latvia went the furthest. On November 1, 1923, they signed a defense treaty under which an unprovoked attack on either country required the other to consider itself at war and provide military assistance. This was a full military alliance, but it included only two small countries. Lithuania remained outside it, Finland kept its distance from formal commitments in the Baltic region, and the earlier plan for a broad alliance that included Poland effectively collapsed. By the mid-1920s, a unified defense bloc stretching from Finland to Poland no longer seemed realistic.
How the Baltic region shifted from a broad alliance to bilateral partnerships
Paradoxically, Finland, which had refused to enter a formal alliance with the Baltic states, soon began close, secret military cooperation with Estonia to prepare for a possible conflict with the Soviet Union. In February 1930, the Finnish and Estonian general staffs discussed jointly closing the Gulf of Finland with minefields and coastal artillery. On November 29, 1932, they approved their first joint military plan. In the years that followed, the two countries held joint coastal defense exercises and expanded cooperation between their navies.
The Finnish-Estonian plan was straightforward. The Soviet Baltic Fleet was based in the eastern Gulf of Finland, primarily around Kronstadt and Leningrad, and had to pass between the Finnish and Estonian coasts to reach the Baltic Sea. The two countries planned to stop it there. Coastal artillery would close the passage with gunfire, while minefields and submarines provided additional defenses. The legacy of the Russian Empire played an important role: before 1917, the empire itself had built the Peter the Great Naval Fortress system on both shores of the Gulf of Finland to defend the approaches to St. Petersburg. Now, some of those fortifications were intended to keep the Soviet fleet from leaving the gulf.
By the late 1930s, the cooperation had become extensive: the general staffs had agreed on a joint military plan, the two countries’ coastal defense forces held joint exercises, and coordination gradually expanded to include their navies. But the partnership had a weak point. But the plans were not backed by a mutual defense treaty that would commit Finland and Estonia to go to war on each other’s behalf. The two countries’ militaries had a clear idea of how they would operate together in a war with the Soviet Union, but no agreement ever formalized those commitments.
The Baltic and Little Ententes: Next attempts at regional alliances
The Baltic states returned to the idea of a broader alliance in the mid-1930s. On September 12, 1934, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania signed the Treaty of Understanding and Cooperation in Geneva, creating what became known as the Baltic Entente. On paper, this was an important step: the three countries pledged to coordinate their foreign policies and hold regular meetings of their foreign ministers. But it did not create a military alliance. The treaty contained no commitment to provide military assistance automatically in the event of an attack.
The reason was the same as before: even a decade and a half after gaining independence, the three countries had different views of the main threats to their security. For Lithuania, the conflict with Poland over Vilnius remained the central issue, while its dispute with Germany over Klaipėda was becoming increasingly acute. Estonia and Latvia did not want to tie their foreign policies to Lithuania’s territorial claims, and the Vilnius issue was explicitly excluded from the Baltic Entente’s joint commitments.
Their attitudes toward the Soviet Union also differed. Estonia and Latvia were much more wary of Moscow, while Lithuania saw the Soviet Union as a potential counterweight to Poland and Germany.
As a result, the Baltic Entente allowed the three countries to coordinate their diplomacy but did not answer the central question: What exactly would they do if one of them had to go to war?
A similar problem emerged farther south in the Little Entente, which consisted of Czechoslovakia, Romania, and Yugoslavia. Created in the early 1920s, the alliance was intended primarily to contain Hungary and prevent a Habsburg restoration. When Germany became the main threat to Czechoslovakia in the 1930s, Prague tried to extend the alliance’s commitments to cover a possible German attack. Romania and Yugoslavia refused. Alliances created to counter the threats of the previous decade proved poorly suited to the new circumstances.
Trial by fire: Why the Baltic states failed to stop the threat from the east
The regional alliances were put to the test just a few years later. After the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact was signed and Poland was partitioned, the Soviet Union began pressuring the Baltic states to allow a Soviet military presence. Estonia was the first: under threat of force, it signed a mutual assistance treaty with the Soviet Union on September 28, 1939, allowing Soviet bases on its territory. Latvia and Lithuania agreed to similar treaties in October. Formally, the three countries remained independent, but their ability to pursue independent policies was significantly reduced.
Finland came next. Moscow demanded border changes on the Karelian Isthmus, the transfer of several islands in the Gulf of Finland, and a Soviet naval base at Hanko. Finland was prepared to make some concessions, but the two sides failed to reach an agreement. On November 30, the Red Army invaded Finland. The countries that had recently discussed their common security now found themselves in completely different situations: Finland was at war with the Soviet Union, while Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were forced to tolerate Soviet troops on their soil.
The contrast was especially stark in the relationship between Finland and Estonia. Not long before, their militaries had been preparing together to trap the Soviet fleet in the Gulf of Finland. Now, the Soviet Union was using bases in Estonia during its war against Finland: Soviet aircraft flew combat missions from these bases, while ships and submarines operated from Estonian ports. Yet the two countries’ military ties did not disappear entirely. Despite the Soviet military presence, Estonian representatives continued to secretly pass intelligence to Finland.
The Baltic Entente formally continued to exist. In December 1939, after the Winter War had already begun, the foreign ministers of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania met in Tallinn for another conference. There, they informally agreed to abstain when the League of Nations considered expelling the Soviet Union over its attack on Finland. In an account sent to Washington, an American diplomat cited the episode as evidence that the three countries had yielded to pressure from Moscow in their foreign policies.
This tragic outcome brought a series of failed attempts to organize a regional alliance to a close. The countries had treaties, diplomatic mechanisms, and even fairly detailed joint military plans. But they never developed a shared understanding of the threats they faced, created a common planning mechanism, or, most importantly, decided in advance under what circumstances each would be willing to go to war for another. Even the Baltic Entente remained a tool for coordinating foreign policy rather than a military alliance.
The final test came in the summer of 1940. In June, the Soviet Union issued ultimatums first to Lithuania and then to Latvia and Estonia, sent in additional troops, and occupied all three countries. Moscow accused the countries, among other things, of turning the Baltic Entente into a military alliance directed against the Soviet Union, thereby violating the mutual assistance treaties they had signed in the fall of 1939. The Baltic states denied that such a military pact existed. The alliance that had proved too weak to ensure the three countries’ collective defense was ultimately used by Moscow as one of the pretexts for ending their independence altogether.
What historical lessons can be learned a century later?
The push for a regional alliance did not fail because the countries misunderstood their vulnerability or made no effort to cooperate. During the 20 years between the world wars, they held dozens of negotiations, signed several treaties, and even developed joint plans for a possible war. The problem lay elsewhere: their cooperation never produced a common understanding of precisely which threat the alliance was meant to deter. The Soviet Union remained the main potential adversary for Estonia and Latvia, while Lithuania was preoccupied with its conflict with Poland. Poland itself feared both Germany and the Soviet Union. Finland, meanwhile, increasingly looked to its Nordic neighbors and pursued neutrality instead of joining a Baltic alliance.
Nor could they resolve the more difficult question of who was truly prepared to fight for a neighbor. Estonia and Latvia made that commitment to each other, while the Finnish and Estonian militaries went so far as to develop detailed joint plans. But no common system stretching from Finland to Poland ever emerged. Ultimately, each country confronted the crisis alone: Poland was defeated and partitioned first; the Soviet Union then attacked Finland; and in the summer of 1940, it occupied and annexed the three Baltic states.
Finally, even closer cooperation could not eliminate the power imbalance between the smaller countries and their larger neighbors. A regional alliance could raise the military cost of an attack and make military operations significantly more difficult for the aggressor, but it could not guarantee that the member states’ own resources would be enough to sustain a prolonged war.
The Baltic region’s interwar history raises a question that remains relevant today: Is combining the forces of small and midsize states sufficient to ensure their collective security, or does a durable system of collective defense require commitments from major outside powers?

articles.title: Airstrikes target Houthi weapons depots in Yemen's Marib: Media
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
15 September 2026•Update: 15 September 2026
Airstrikes targeted weapons depots belonging to Yemen’s Houthi group in the central Marib province, according to Yemeni media on Tuesday.
The pro-government West Coast news platform said the strikes hit Houthi weapons depots in the Al-Jubah district, without providing details on casualties or damage.
In a separate development in Marib, Yemeni government forces foiled a Houthi infiltration attempt in the Harib district, the outlet said.
In another incident, the media arm of the Taiz military command said warplanes struck a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform at Taiz airport.
Local sources also reported airstrikes targeting a meeting of Houthi leaders at the local council building in Khadir, east of Taiz.
The reported attacks come amid escalating fighting between the Houthis and government-aligned forces. In recent weeks, airstrikes have also targeted Houthi positions, reinforcements and missile-launching sites in Taiz province.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.

articles.title: Ukrainian Attack Kills One in Belgorod, Hits Commercial and Industrial Sites Across Russia
articles.body:
Overnight Ukrainian drone and missile strikes across southern Russia killed one person and struck commercial and industrial sites, regional officials said Tuesday.
Acting Belgorod region Governor Alexander Shuvayev confirmed one death in an attack near the border with Ukraine. He also said that a woman who was hospitalized for her injuries following strikes earlier this month had died.
In the nearby Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar said an Ozon warehouse was among several sites damaged during a missile attack on the port city of Taganrog.
Ozon confirmed that it suspended operations at the facility, where it said a fire broke out. No one was hurt, the company said.
Federal investigators launched a criminal probe into terrorism over the attacks on Taganrog, citing damage to Ozon and other residential and agricultural buildings.
Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said an “industrial facility” was damaged in overnight strikes. Unconfirmed reports said that a fire broke out at the Syzran Oil Refinery.
NASA’s fire monitoring service FIRMS showed an active fire Tuesday morning on the southwestern outskirts of Syzran, where the refinery, which has been attacked multiple times this year, is located.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 222 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Monday night and Tuesday morning.
In Ukraine, officials said one person was killed in Russian attacks on Kyiv. Separate attacks on the city of Zaporizhzhia also killed one person.
Two gas stations in Kyiv were damaged in the overnight strikes, the state energy company Naftogaz said.
The attacks targeting energy infrastructure in both Russia and Ukraine came despite an announcement by U.S. Donald Trump earlier in the week that the two warring sides allegedly agreed to pause such attacks.
Trump has sought to blame the surging cost of diesel in the United States on Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil refineries. While those attacks have put pressure on fuel prices both inside Russia and globally, so too has the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran led to major disruptions in energy markets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday that Trump’s suggestion for a ceasefire on energy sites, which has been repeatedly floated over the past year, was a “very good idea” but alone would not bring down global fuel costs.

articles.title: Republican Congressman Introduces Articles of Impeachment Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.body:
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie has moved to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, marking perhaps the most striking instance yet of a member of President Donald Trump’s own party publicly condemning one of his top Cabinet officials.
The Kentucky Congressman introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Tuesday, including allegations that the Defense Secretary is waging the war in Iran in contravention of multiple provisions of the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
One of the articles of impeachment also alleges that Hegseth is “suppressing free speech” by using the Defense Department’s “authority to retaliate against and intimidate Senator Mark Kelly for constitutionally protected speech,” after the lawmaker made a video with other Democrats reminding members of the military and intelligence community that they can refuse to carry out illegal orders.
Another article that Massie introduced alleges that the U.S. military operation in Venezuela that led to the capture of President Nicolas Maduro and his wife was carried out “without constitutional or legal authority.”
“By engaging in hostilities in Iran for more than 90 days without congressional authorization, Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said in a statement. “Secretary Hegseth’s constitutional violations extend beyond the illegal war in Iran. He is abusing the power of his office to ignore congressional war powers resolutions, to kidnap foreign leaders, and to intimidate critics of the Trump administration by retaliating against them for exercising free speech.”
“If we are to remain true to our oath to ‘support and defend the Constitution of the United States,’ Congress must not turn a blind eye to Secretary Hegseth’s unconstitutional and illegal actions,” Massie continued.
Massie said to reporters on Tuesday that he didn’t tell Republican leaders ahead of time that he was going to make such a move. The impeachment push faces a steep uphill battle given GOP control over the House. And even if the resolution were to make it through the lower chamber, a two-thirds majority vote in the Republican-controlled Senate would be required to convict Hegseth in order to expel him from office, likely making the effort dead on arrival.
It’s not yet clear when exactly the House will vote on Massie’s resolution; the lower chamber is scheduled to leave the nation’s capital later this week for a recess.
Massie’s move to impeach Hegseth comes as the Defense Secretary has faced widespread backlash—from Democrats and some Republicans—over issues such as the Iran war and his internal management of the Pentagon. Earlier this month, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina called on the President to replace Hegseth, after Dan Driscoll stepped down as Army Secretary—one of at least 20 military and civilian leaders who have been ousted or resigned from the Department of Defense since Hegseth took over the agency.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said in a social media post. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force.”
“I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it,” the North Carolina Senator continued.
Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican from Nebraska, told CNN that he agreed “with the sentiments” that Tillis had expressed, though he didn’t explicitly urge Trump to fire Hegseth.
“I hate to tell the President who he should hire and fire. I don’t know if it’s really my role, but I would say this: I would not—[Hegseth] would not be on my team. I think he is—he has not been a very good leader in many ways,” Bacon said. “I wouldn’t hire him myself.”
Despite these Republicans’ criticisms of Hegseth, the President has continued to throw his support behind the Defense Secretary, saying that Hegseth is “doing a fantastic job” in the role.
When asked about Massie’s measure during a press conference on Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche replied, “Secretary Hegseth is doing a phenomenal job” and went on to say that “the Secretary of War doesn’t just go off and do things—he follows the law.”
This isn’t the first time that Massie has clashed with the White House. Massie strongly voiced his opposition to the President’s “One Big Beautiful Bill” and criticized Trump’s actions in Venezuela. Massie also joined Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna to lead the push for the Department of Justice to release the files connected to the investigation into the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein—an effort that Trump long objected to before ultimately signing the legislation into law last year after it was passed by Congress.
Trump publicly attacked the Kentucky lawmaker for months, calling him “the Worst ‘Republican’ Congressman we have had in many years” and “a totally ineffective LOSER who has failed us so badly.” The President endorsed and campaigned for Massie’s primary opponent Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat the lawmaker in May.

articles.title: Germany’s secretive ‘Sonderstab Ukraine’ fast-tracks weapons deals for Kyiv in as little as two weeks, FT reports
articles.body:
Germany’s secretive ‘Sonderstab Ukraine’ fast-tracks weapons deals for Kyiv in as little as two weeks, FT reports
A small, standalone unit inside Germany’s Defense Ministry known as the “Sonderstab Ukraine” can arrange weapons deals for Kyiv in just two weeks — a fraction of the time other departments take when bogged down by the bureaucracy of domestic procurement, the Financial Times reports.
The unit’s head, Brigadier General Joachim Kaschke, said, “We have extremely short decision-making chains. That makes us agile and flexible.”
The Ukraine unit was formed in 2022, a few months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and quickly earned a reputation as a responsive, efficient body, the FT writes. Because Ukraine’s government — not Germany’s — signed the contracts, the unit sidestepped German procurement rules.
Since then, the unit’s role has shifted several times as Germany moved from cautious support to becoming one of Kyiv’s main partners. Over the past year, the Sonderstab has become a hub where the German and Ukrainian defense ministries and defense companies exchange experience and technology.
The unit remains compact today, employing fewer than 20 people. “It’s got a bit of a start-up vibe,” said a source familiar with the team’s work. “They have a very deep knowledge of systems: what works . . . and what is overpriced, glitzy nonsense.”
Germany is one of Ukraine’s key allies. In September, German authorities decided to transfer some of their own stockpiled anti-aircraft missiles for American Patriot air defense systems to Ukraine, which needs them to repel Russian missile strikes. A recent ARD-Deutschlandtrend poll showed that 39% of respondents in western Germany consider weapons deliveries to Ukraine excessive, compared with 54% in the east.

articles.title: Zaluzhny: desire to de-occupy territories using Soviet methods drove mobilization into deadlock
articles.body:
Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of Ukraine to the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–24) Valeriy Zaluzhny has noted that the Russian-Ukrainian war has become not only a war of technologies, but also a war of strategies and doctrines that change under the pressure of progress, and therefore it is a major mistake to obsess over individual technologies and their PR, which complements Soviet strategy and requires Soviet-type executors.
"It was precisely the desire to de-occupy territories and hold them using Soviet methods and strategies, only with new weapons, that drove mobilization into a deadlock. Mobilization provided only one chance, and there were fewer and fewer willing to take it. For we are unable to endure a war of machines against a huge Soviet country where people are essentially turned into machines and thrown to fight against real machines... It is necessary, while recognizing technologies as a new weapon, to remember the patterns of the development of military art and invariably form new forms and methods of their application based on this. And only after that should organizational changes be carried out in the structure of the Armed Forces that apply this new weapon in new forms and methods. It is precisely in this place that mobilization is located as part of a new strategy based on new weapons and precisely new, rather than Soviet, forms and methods of application," Zaluzhny wrote in his article published in Ukrainska Pravda on Tuesday.
He emphasized that between Ukraine and Russia it is no longer a war of drones, since drones "have transformed into forms of weaponry more familiar to us from the past, lowering costs and availability while increasing effectiveness."
According to the diplomat, the old rules no longer apply, and therefore modern warfare requires new doctrines, while Ukraine is already experiencing the pressure of "known intermediaries" on itself due to the introduction of a new approach to waging war, without specifying who is meant. "Meanwhile, a war of technologies is already underway, and Ukraine is already experiencing systemic pressure, which is the result of implementing not only technologies, but also a new doctrinal approach to their application, including production and research as an integral part of strategy. This very thing gives Russia the right to issue ultimatums to us through known intermediaries. This is precisely what is directed at and can lead to a whole series of crises," Zaluzhny writes.
He stressed that a war of attrition "is not only battles, but also societal breakdowns, the main thing being who causes them first."
"To find a way out of an entirely natural situation, an understanding of the search for and implementation of precisely a systemic response to Russia's pressure is needed. This systemic response must be based on building such a strategy where joint production and the implementation of new technological solutions must become part of systemic steps both for defense and for influencing Russia's ability to continue the war. For this, of course, the search remains urgent for precisely resource and technological alliances capable of ensuring this production, including to satisfy our own defense needs. This production must be doctrinally included as part of the victory strategy, where it is not a magical model of weaponry that is produced, but the entire necessary new arsenal, including civilian-purpose items in accordance with the conditions of progress," Zaluzhny summarized.

articles.title: Ukraine to Boost Protection of Railways, Fuel Stations
articles.body:
Ukraine will strengthen protection for railways, gas stations and other critical enterprises against Russian attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
Zelensky made the announcement after a meeting of Ukraine’s top military command, where officials discussed contracts for systems protecting critical infrastructure and logistics.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine to expand electronic warfare and air defense
Officials reviewed the security needs of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s national railway operator, fuel station networks and other facilities identified as priority targets for Russian strikes.
“Solutions for protection exist,” Zelensky said. “In particular, we will significantly strengthen the electronic warfare component and increase procurement volumes. The contracts have been confirmed.”
The president said mobile fire groups and air-defense lines protecting designated facilities would also be reorganized. He did not disclose details of the protection plans.
The meeting came amid continued Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy and logistics infrastructure, including strikes on fuel stations in Kyiv. Kyiv has said that Russia’s campaign against critical infrastructure is continuing despite discussions about a possible pause in energy strikes. Previously, Moscow and Kyiv had not agreed on formal terms for such a truce.
Backup logistics routes planned for frontline regions
Zelensky instructed the Finance Ministry to provide additional resources for logistics needs and thanked international partners helping maintain uninterrupted railway operations.
Russian Forces Use Artificial Intelligence to Show Artificial Victory
Officials also discussed railway security in border areas near European Union countries and Moldova, as well as support for Ukrzaliznytsia’s rolling-stock repairs and equipment supplies.
The government is preparing backup logistics routes for frontline regions, including plans to combine rail and bus transport when necessary.
“Details are not public,” Zelensky said of updated measures to protect critical infrastructure.
